t: MFA and passwordless: TOTP, push, SMS weaknesses, WebAuthn and passkeys, phishing resistance and account recovery
sum: Second factors and their failure modes: a TOTP code computed by hand from a secret and a timestamp (RFC 6238), why codes and push prompts are phishable in real time (Cloudflare 2022, Uber's MFA fatigue, Retool's synced codes), SMS and SIM swaps, how WebAuthn and passkeys bind a signature to the origin so phishing fails, synced vs device-bound passkeys and NIST AAL3, rolling MFA out, and account recovery as the weakest link.
prereq: au2
Passwords leak through reuse and phishing; credential stuffing replays them at scale; HMAC is a keyed hash; online guessing is limited by rate limits.
au3
A session cookie is a bearer credential that bypasses passwords and MFA once issued; step-up asks for fresh authentication before sensitive actions.
au1
NIST SP 800-63B-4 defines AAL1-AAL3; AAL2 must offer a phishing-resistant option and AAL3 requires one with a non-exportable key.
net9
Public-key signatures: a private key signs, the public key verifies; TLS binds a connection to a domain name the browser has checked.
why:
On 20 July 2022, more than a hundred Cloudflare employees and family members received text messages telling them their work schedules had changed, with a link to a convincing copy of Cloudflare's Okta login page on a freshly registered domain. At least 76 employees received them; three typed in their usernames and passwords. The phishing kit was built to beat two-factor authentication: as soon as a victim entered credentials, they were relayed to the attacker through Telegram, and when the real site asked for a one-time code, the fake page asked the victim for it and relayed that too, inside its 30-second window. Against most companies' MFA, those three people would have handed over working sessions.

Nothing happened. Every Cloudflare employee logged in with a FIDO2 hardware security key, and a security key doesn't produce a code that can be relayed. It signs a challenge together with the address of the site that's asking — and the site asking was the phishing domain. The signature was useless at the real login page. Around the same time the same attackers went after Twilio, and researchers later linked the campaign to well over a hundred targeted organisations; where employees typed codes, it got in.

Two months after that, Uber was breached when an attacker who had a contractor's password triggered push approval prompts over and over until the contractor accepted one. In 2023, Retool lost control of an employee account after an SMS phish and a deepfaked phone call — and discovered the employee's authenticator codes had been synced to the same Google account the attacker then controlled.

All three companies "had MFA". What separated them is what kind. This topic explains the second factors in use today from the inside — computing a TOTP code by hand from a secret and a timestamp, then seeing why codes and push prompts fall to real-time phishing, why SMS is classified as restricted, and how WebAuthn and passkeys bind a login to the website's origin so that phishing simply fails. Then it deals with the part attackers increasingly target instead: enrolment, lost devices and account recovery, which are only as strong as their weakest path.
primer:
Two kinds of proof

Imagine two ways to prove to a bank teller that you're you over the phone. In the first, you and the bank agreed on a secret codebook years ago; the teller asks for today's code and you read it out. In the second, you have a sealing ring; the teller reads you a random phrase plus the name of the bank, you seal a letter containing both and post it, and the teller checks the seal against the impression on file.

Now a con artist calls you pretending to be the bank. With the codebook, you read today's code to the con artist, who immediately reads it to the real bank: you've been relayed. With the ring, the con artist reads you a phrase — but your letter says the name of whoever actually asked, and the ring is engraved to only seal letters naming your real bank. The con artist gets a letter that the real bank will refuse. That's the difference between codes (TOTP, SMS, email codes) and origin-bound signatures (WebAuthn). Both are "something you have"; only the second is phishing-resistant.

Where the analogy breaks: in WebAuthn you don't check the name yourself — the browser writes the real origin into what's signed, so it works even when the fake site looks perfect. People can't reliably spot phishing; the design doesn't ask them to.

Why a second factor at all

A password is one secret, typed into many places, remembered by a human and reused across sites — every weakness in au2 follows from that. A second factor adds evidence of a different kind, so an attacker who has the password still lacks something. The categories are something you know, something you have and something you are; MFA means two different categories, so a password plus a security question is still one factor. In practice "something you have" is a phone or a security key holding a secret or a private key, and "something you are" is a fingerprint or face check that unlocks that key locally. The question for the rest of this topic is how each kind of "have" can be stolen, copied or talked out of its owner.

The landscape in one table

MethodWhat the user doesPhishable in real time?Main weakness
SMS / voice codetypes a texted codeyesSIM swap, interception
Email code / linktypes a code or clicksyesemail account compromise
TOTP apptypes a 6-digit codeyesrelay; shared secret on server
Push approvaltaps Approveyes (fatigue, relay)approving the attacker's login
WebAuthn / passkeytouches key or unlocks devicenorecovery paths, session theft

Every row beats a password alone against credential stuffing (au2), which is still the bulk of attacks on consumer accounts. The ranking matters when the attacker is targeting you specifically, with a phishing page.

If you stop here: codes and taps stop password reuse but not a targeted phish; origin-bound passkeys and security keys stop both; and whatever you deploy, the recovery path decides your real security level.
body:
1. One-time passwords from a shared secret: HOTP

The code-generating apps (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password and many others) implement two RFCs. HOTP (RFC 4226, 2005) defines a code from a shared secret K and a counter C:

HOTP(K, C) = Truncate(HMAC-SHA1(K, C)) mod 10^digits

C is an 8-byte big-endian integer. HMAC-SHA1 (the keyed hash from au4, with SHA-1 inside) gives 20 bytes. Dynamic truncation turns them into a short number: take the low 4 bits of the last byte as an offset (0-15), read the 4 bytes starting at that offset as a big-endian integer, clear the top bit (so the result is a non-negative 31-bit number regardless of signed arithmetic), and reduce modulo 106 for six digits. With a counter, both sides must stay in sync — each button press advances it — which is awkward, so most systems use time instead.

2. TOTP, computed by hand

TOTP (RFC 6238, 2011) replaces the counter with the number of 30-second steps since the Unix epoch: T = floor(unix_time / 30). Both sides compute the same T as long as their clocks roughly agree.

Let's compute one. Enrolment gave the user a QR code containing otpauth://totp/Example:ada?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP&issuer=Example. The secret is in base32 (letters A-Z and digits 2-7, chosen so it can be typed without ambiguity). JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP decodes to the 10 bytes 48 65 6c 6c 6f 21 de ad be ef — "Hello!" followed by 0xDEADBEEF, a well-known demo secret. (Real secrets are 20 random bytes; RFC 4226 requires at least 16 and recommends 20.)

The time is 2026-10-07 08:00:00 UTC, Unix time 1791360000.

  1. Time step. T = floor(1791360000 / 30) = 59,712,000 = 0x038F2200.
  2. Counter bytes. 8 bytes big-endian: 00 00 00 00 03 8f 22 00.
  3. HMAC. HMAC-SHA1(secret, counter) = b9 b2 3b fc 66 b4 1e 21 a0 a3 f0 54 b4 a6 ea 0f b9 9f a3 15.
  4. Offset. The last byte is 0x15; its low 4 bits are 0x5, so offset = 5.
  5. Four bytes from offset 5. Bytes 5-8 are b4 1e 21 a0 = 0xB41E21A0.
  6. Clear the top bit. 0xB41E21A0 & 0x7FFFFFFF = 0x341E21A0 = 874,389,920.
  7. Six digits. 874,389,920 mod 1,000,000 = 389920.

The authenticator app shows 389920 from 08:00:00 to 08:00:29. The codes for the steps either side are 560726 (07:59:30) and 529698 (08:00:30). You can check an implementation against RFC 6238's own test vector: with the ASCII secret 12345678901234567890, time 59 seconds and 8 digits, SHA-1 gives 94287082.

3. Verifying TOTP on the server

The server stores the shared secret for each user (encrypted — it's equivalent to the authenticator) and, on login, computes codes for T−1, T and T+1 to tolerate clock drift and typing time. Three details matter:

  • Replay. A code is valid for its whole step. Record the last accepted T per user and reject codes for that step or earlier, or a code shoulder-surfed or captured from a log can be reused within seconds.
  • Rate limiting. With three acceptable codes at any moment, each guess succeeds with probability 3 in 106. With NIST's cap of 100 consecutive failures, an attacker's total chance is about 100 × 3×10−6 = 0.03%. Without limits, 10 guesses a second for a day is 864,000 guesses, and 1 − (1 − 3×10−6)864,000 ≈ 1 − e−2.59 ≈ 92%. Six digits are safe only because attempts are limited per account.
  • Secret handling. The secret appears once, in the enrolment QR code; confirm enrolment by asking for one valid code, then never display it again. Because the server holds it, a database breach that includes TOTP secrets lets an attacker generate every user's codes — unlike passkeys, where the server holds only public keys.

4. Push approvals and their failure modes

Push MFA sends a notification to an enrolled app: "Approve sign-in?" The user taps Approve, and the app signs the approval with a key it holds. It's convenient and the cryptography is sound. The weakness is the human step. In MFA fatigue (or "push bombing"), an attacker who has the password triggers approval after approval — late at night, dozens of times — until the user taps Approve to make it stop, or believes a follow-up message from "IT" saying to accept it. Uber's September 2022 breach began this way: the attacker repeatedly tried to log in to a contractor's account, each attempt sent an approval request, and eventually the contractor accepted one.

Push is also relayable: a phishing page can trigger the real site's push at the moment the victim expects one, and the victim approves the attacker's session believing it's their own.

Mitigations: number matching — the login page displays a two-digit number that the user must type into the app — ties the approval to the screen in front of the user (it doesn't stop a relay where the phishing page shows the number, but it stops blind approvals and fatigue); show the requesting location, device and application in the prompt; rate-limit pushes and alert security on bursts; give users a "deny and report" button that locks the login. Treat push as a convenience factor, not a phishing defence.

5. SMS, voice and email codes

SMS codes are TOTP's weaker cousin: the server generates a random code and texts it. They add the phone network to the attack surface. SIM swapping — persuading or bribing a mobile carrier's staff to move a number to a SIM the attacker holds — gives the attacker every subsequent text. Number porting to another carrier does the same. Weaknesses in the SS7 signalling network between carriers have been used to intercept messages, and phone malware can read them. NIST SP 800-63B-4 designates authentication through the public switched telephone network as restricted: allowed, but verifiers must offer an alternative and assess the risk. Email codes inherit the security of the user's mailbox, which is often protected by nothing more than a reused password.

The honest summary: SMS stops credential stuffing (the attacker has the password but not the phone) and fails against targeted attacks. It's acceptable as a consumer baseline where nothing better is adopted and wrong for administrators.

6. WebAuthn: public-key login bound to the origin

WebAuthn (W3C Web Authentication; Level 3 became a W3C Recommendation on 25 August 2026) is a browser API that lets a website create and use public-key credentials. Together with CTAP — the protocol between the browser and external authenticators such as USB security keys — it makes up the FIDO Alliance's FIDO2. The parts:

  • The relying party (RP) is the website, identified by an RP ID, normally its registrable domain such as example.com.
  • The authenticator holds private keys: a roaming authenticator (a security key over USB, NFC or Bluetooth) or a platform authenticator built into the device (Windows Hello, Apple's Touch ID/Face ID with iCloud Keychain, Android's screen lock with Google Password Manager), or a password manager acting as one.
  • The credential is a key pair created for one RP ID; the RP stores the public key and a credential ID.

Registration (navigator.credentials.create()): the server sends a random challenge, its RP ID and name, a user handle (an opaque user ID, not an email) and acceptable algorithms (COSE identifiers: −7 for ES256, −8 for EdDSA, −257 for RS256). The authenticator creates a new key pair scoped to that RP ID, checks the user is present (a touch) and optionally verifies them (PIN or biometric), and returns the public key and credential ID, optionally with an attestation — a signed statement about the authenticator model, useful in enterprises that only allow certain hardware. The server checks the challenge and origin, then stores credential ID, public key, signature counter and flags.

Authentication (navigator.credentials.get()): the server sends a fresh challenge (and optionally the allowed credential IDs). The browser builds clientDataJSON:

{"type":"webauthn.get",
 "challenge":"q8E3…(base64url of the server's random bytes)",
 "origin":"https://example.com","crossOrigin":false}

The authenticator finds a credential for the RP ID, checks presence (and verification if requested), and signs:

authenticatorData = SHA-256("example.com")  (32 bytes, the RP ID hash)
                  ‖ flags (1 byte: UP, UV, BE, BS, …)
                  ‖ signCount (4 bytes)
signature = Sign(private key, authenticatorData ‖ SHA-256(clientDataJSON))

The server verifies: the challenge is one it issued and hasn't expired or been used; type is webauthn.get; origin is exactly its own origin; the RP ID hash equals SHA-256 of its RP ID; the flags meet policy — UP (user present) always, UV (user verified) if it wants two factors in one; the signature verifies with the stored public key; and the signature counter has increased if the authenticator uses one (a counter going backwards suggests a cloned authenticator; synced passkeys often report 0).

Why phishing fails. Two independent bindings. The authenticator only uses a credential on the RP ID it was created for, and the browser only lets a page request RP IDs matching its own domain — so on examp1e-login.com the real site's credential is simply unavailable. And even if an attacker proxies the real site's challenge, the browser writes the phishing page's origin into clientDataJSON, which is inside the signature, and the real server rejects it. The user doesn't need to notice anything. That's the formal meaning of phishing-resistant: the authenticator output can't be relayed to the real site from anywhere else.

Note what the server stores: a public key. A database breach gives the attacker nothing to log in with and nothing to crack.

7. Passkeys

A passkey is the consumer name for a FIDO/WebAuthn discoverable credential — one stored on the authenticator together with the user handle, so the site can ask "any credential for example.com?" without the user typing a username first. With user verification, a passkey is a whole login in one step: possession of the device's key plus the local PIN or biometric is two factors. Two kinds matter for policy:

  • Synced passkeys are copied across a user's devices by their platform or password manager, protected by end-to-end encryption tied to the user's cloud account. Lose the phone, and the passkey is on the laptop and the new phone. WebAuthn's flags report this: BE (backup eligible) and BS (backed up).
  • Device-bound passkeys live only in one device's secure hardware — a hardware security key, or a platform key marked non-syncable. Lose the device, and the credential is gone.

NIST SP 800-63B-4 accepts syncable authenticators at AAL2 but says they shall not be used at AAL3, which requires a non-exportable private key. The usual policy follows: synced passkeys for customers and most employees (they fix recovery, the biggest practical problem with hardware keys), two hardware keys each for administrators and anyone with production access.

Can this app use passkeys? Indirectly, yes: the Prep Console has no passwords and delegates authentication to Google and GitHub, both of which support passkeys and security keys. A user who protects their Google account with a passkey gets phishing-resistant sign-in to the Prep Console without the app doing anything. That's one of federation's real benefits (au6): the strongest authenticator the IdP supports becomes available to every relying application.

8. Enrolment and recovery: the weakest link

Every MFA system has three doors besides the login: enrolment (adding a factor), removal (deleting one) and recovery (getting in when factors are lost). Attackers go for whichever is weakest.

  • Enrolment must require an existing strong factor (or happen during a verified onboarding). If a session from a phished password can add a new authenticator, MFA protects nothing — Retool's attacker added their own device to the employee's Okta account.
  • Recovery codes: show 8-10 single-use random codes at enrolment, store them hashed like passwords (au2), and let users regenerate them.
  • Multiple authenticators: encourage or require two (a phone passkey and a hardware key, or synced passkeys on two devices), so losing one isn't a recovery event.
  • Slow paths for true loss: identity verification, a waiting period of a day or more with notifications to every registered channel so the real owner can cancel, and limits on what a freshly recovered account can do immediately (no payout or email changes).
  • Help desks: scripted verification that doesn't rely on knowledge an attacker can research or a voice that can be faked; for privileged accounts, in-person or video verification plus manager approval. Retool's attacker used a deepfaked voice of a member of IT staff.
  • Synced secrets: if TOTP seeds sync to the same cloud account that a password unlocks, the second factor collapses into the first. Retool's write-up describes exactly that with Google Authenticator's cloud sync.
deep:
What exactly makes WebAuthn phishing-resistant — and what doesn't

Phishing resistance comes from the browser, not the cryptography alone. The browser enforces that a page at origin O can only request credentials for RP IDs that are O's domain or a registrable suffix of it, and it writes O into clientDataJSON. An attacker who controls the browser (malware), or a native app that implements its own WebAuthn client without those checks, can break the binding — which is why platforms require apps to prove association with a domain (Apple's associated domains, Android's Digital Asset Links) before they can use that domain's passkeys. Similarly, an attacker who controls a subdomain of the RP ID can request the parent's credentials, because RP IDs are domain-scoped; keep untrusted content off subdomains of your RP ID (the same advice as for SameSite cookies in au3). And phishing resistance protects the login; it does nothing about a session stolen afterwards by infostealer malware, which is why device-bound sessions (au3) are the natural companion.

Attestation: when to care

Attestation lets an authenticator prove its model (via an AAGUID and a certificate chain from the manufacturer, checked against the FIDO Metadata Service). Consumer sites generally request no attestation: it adds friction, leaks device information and excludes users. Enterprises and regulated environments use it to require specific certified hardware — for example to meet AAL3, where the RP must know the key is non-exportable. Synced passkey providers usually return no attestation, which is itself a signal that the key isn't hardware-bound.

Signature counters and cloned authenticators

WebAuthn authenticators may include a counter that increments with each signature. If the server sees a counter lower than or equal to the stored one, the credential may have been cloned (two copies signing independently). For hardware keys that's a useful tripwire. Synced passkeys legitimately exist on several devices, so they typically report a counter of 0, and servers must not treat that as cloning. Policy should key off the BE/BS flags: for device-bound credentials, enforce counter monotonicity; for synced ones, ignore it.

Conditional UI and passkey adoption

Adoption depends on UX. WebAuthn's "conditional mediation" lets the browser offer passkeys in the username field's autofill dropdown, so users who have a passkey just pick it, and users who don't see an ordinary form. Combined with prompts to create a passkey after a password login, this lets sites migrate gradually without a hard switch. The security payoff arrives only when the password path is removed or demoted for users who have passkeys; otherwise attackers simply phish the password path. Measure the fraction of logins that used a phishing-resistant method, not the fraction of users who registered one.

Risk-based and adaptive authentication

Not every login needs the strongest factor. Adaptive systems score each attempt — known device cookie, IP reputation, impossible travel, time of day, recent failures — and decide whether to skip, require or step up MFA. Done well, it reduces friction for routine logins and concentrates challenges on suspicious ones. Done badly, it becomes an oracle (attackers probe until they find conditions that skip MFA) and a source of inconsistency. Risk signals should only ever add requirements to a baseline policy, never remove the requirement for privileged access.

The economics of attacks on MFA

Every step up the hierarchy changes the attacker's cost structure. Against passwords alone, attacks are automated and scale to millions of accounts (credential stuffing). SMS and TOTP force attackers to phish in real time or SIM-swap — still automatable with phishing kits, but per-victim. Push forces a live interaction with the victim. Origin-bound credentials force attackers to compromise the device itself or a recovery path, which is expensive and noisy. Real attacker behaviour follows: kits for relaying codes are sold as a service, help-desk social engineering has grown as phishing-resistant MFA spreads, and session-cookie theft by infostealers bypasses MFA entirely. A senior answer names where the attacker will go next once you deploy each control.

Passwordless without passkeys: magic links

"Passwordless" also describes email magic links and one-time codes by email. They remove passwords (and so credential stuffing) but move all security to the user's email account and are phishable: an attacker can trigger a code and ask the victim to read it out. Treat them as convenience login equivalent to an email-based factor, keep links short-lived and single-use, bind them to the browser that requested them where possible (so a link opened on another device asks for confirmation), and don't treat them as MFA on their own.
prod:
What goes wrong in deployments

Fallback paths that undo the upgrade. A company deploys security keys but leaves "send me a code instead" enabled; phishing kits simply choose the code path. Inventory every way to satisfy MFA per user and remove the weak ones for high-risk groups.

Enrolment hijack. New-device enrolment allowed with only a password, or by help-desk ticket; attackers phish the password, enrol their own authenticator, and now hold a legitimate factor. Require an existing strong factor or verified identity for enrolment, and alert the user on every new authenticator.

Clock drift breaking TOTP for users whose phones have the wrong time; widen the window slightly or show a clear error, never widen it to minutes.

Lost-device floods after a hardware-key rollout without second keys — the help desk drowns and is tempted to shortcut verification. Ship two keys, or pair a key with a synced passkey.

Push bombing: a user reports dozens of prompts at 2 a.m. Treat it as a confirmed password compromise: force a password change, revoke sessions, and check for any approved prompt.

Metrics

Share of logins by method (password-only, SMS, TOTP, push, WebAuthn); share of privileged logins using phishing-resistant methods (target 100%); MFA challenge failure rate and push denial rate; push requests per user per hour (fatigue detection); new-authenticator enrolments and removals per day; recovery requests and their approval rate; time from report to lock for "this wasn't me".

The three cases, read as engineers

Cloudflare, July 2022: SMS phishing to at least 76 employees, three entered credentials, a kit relayed credentials and codes via Telegram in real time and attempted to install AnyDesk remote-access software; every employee used FIDO2 keys with origin binding, so no account was compromised. Cloudflare then blocked the phishing domain and searched for affected devices. Uber, September 2022: a contractor's credentials were stolen (Uber believes via malware on a personal device); repeated login attempts each sent a push approval, and the contractor eventually accepted one. Retool, August 2023: SMS phishing led an employee to a fake portal, a deepfaked voice call impersonating IT obtained an MFA code, the attacker added their own device to the employee's Okta account, and Google Authenticator's cloud sync meant compromising the employee's Google account exposed their codes; 27 cloud customers were affected. Together they draw the hierarchy this topic teaches: codes are relayed, pushes are approved, synced secrets inherit their account's weakness, and only origin-bound keys held.

Talking to users

Users need to know three things, and most products tell them none: what a legitimate prompt looks like (and that you will never phone them for a code), what to do when they get a prompt they didn't trigger (deny and report, with one tap), and what happens when they lose a device (the recovery path and how long it takes). Clear messaging reduces both fatigue approvals and help-desk pressure to shortcut verification.

Rollout guidance

Start with the accounts whose compromise is catastrophic (identity-provider admins, cloud root, CI/CD, finance), give them two hardware keys and remove all other methods for them. Then move all employees to passkeys with a sunset date for codes. For customers, offer passkeys with conditional UI and prompts after login, keep TOTP for those who want it, and treat SMS as a last resort. Throughout, harden enrolment and recovery first — otherwise each improvement just redirects attackers to the help desk.
myths: Any MFA stops phishing.

Codes from an app, SMS or email can be typed into a phishing page and relayed to the real site within seconds — Cloudflare's 2022 attackers built exactly that, relaying codes over Telegram. Push prompts can be approved by a tired or tricked user. Only origin-bound methods — WebAuthn passkeys and security keys, or client certificates — fail on a phishing site, because the browser won't produce a valid signature for the wrong origin.
SMS codes are as good as an authenticator app.

SMS travels through the phone network and the carrier's account systems: SIM-swap fraud (convincing a carrier to move your number), number porting, SS7 interception and malware on the phone all expose it. NIST SP 800-63B-4 classifies PSTN-based out-of-band authentication as 'restricted'. It's still much better than nothing against credential stuffing, but it shouldn't protect high-value accounts.
Passkeys are just a nicer password manager.

A password manager stores a shared secret that the site also knows and that the user can type anywhere. A passkey is a private key that never leaves the authenticator (or the user's synced keychain), with only the public key on the server; each login is a fresh signature over a server challenge and the origin. There's nothing reusable to steal from the server and nothing the user can be tricked into typing.
Biometric login means the site gets my fingerprint.

With WebAuthn the fingerprint or face check happens on the device and only unlocks the private key locally (user verification). The site receives a signature and a flag saying verification happened, never biometric data.
Once MFA is on, the account is safe.

Attackers go around it: steal the session cookie after login (au3), call the help desk to reset MFA, compromise the account that holds synced codes (Retool 2023), or abuse a recovery flow that asks for less than the login did. The security of an account is the security of its weakest recovery path.
lab:
Goal: implement HOTP/TOTP from the RFCs and a server-side verifier with replay protection and rate limits, using Python 3.12's standard library (hmac, hashlib, struct, base64, time). About 15 minutes.

  1. HOTP. Write hotp(key, counter, digits=6): struct.pack(">Q", counter), hmac.new(key, msg, "sha1").digest(), offset h[-1] & 0x0F, struct.unpack(">I", h[o:o+4])[0] & 0x7FFFFFFF, modulo 10**digits.
  2. RFC check. TOTP with key b"12345678901234567890", time 59, 8 digits must give 94287082.
  3. This lesson's code. base64.b32decode("JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP"), time 1791360000 → 389920; times 1791359970 and 1791360030 → 560726 and 529698. Print the intermediate HMAC and offset and compare with the body.
  4. Your phone. Generate a 20-byte secret with secrets.token_bytes(20), base32 it, build the otpauth://totp/Lab:you?secret=…&issuer=Lab URI and type the secret into an authenticator app (or render a QR code if you have a tool). Compare its codes with yours for a minute.
  5. Verifier. verify(user, code, now) accepts T−1..T+1, rejects any T ≤ the user's last accepted step (replay), and locks after 5 consecutive failures with exponential backoff.
  6. Guessing. Simulate an attacker sending random codes at your verifier without the lockout for 100,000 attempts and count successes; then with it.

What to look for: steps 2-3 reproduce the RFC vector and the lesson's numbers exactly. Step 4 matches a real authenticator app, proving there's no magic. Step 5 rejects the same code twice in one window. Step 6 finds roughly 0.3 successes per 100,000 guesses (3 × 10−6 each) without lockout — near-certain success over a day at scale — and essentially none with it.
recap: MFA requires evidence from two different factor categories, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
TOTP (RFC 6238) is HMAC-SHA1 of the number of 30-second steps since 1970, dynamically truncated to 6 digits; both sides share the secret, so it's phishable and the server must protect the secret.
Push approvals are phishable and vulnerable to fatigue; number matching and context reduce but don't remove the risk.
SMS and voice codes are exposed to SIM swaps, porting and interception, and NIST classifies them as restricted.
WebAuthn signs a server challenge together with the origin and RP ID using a key scoped to the site, so a phishing page can't obtain a usable assertion; this is what phishing-resistant means.
Passkeys are discoverable WebAuthn credentials; synced passkeys survive device loss but have exportable keys (not AAL3), while device-bound security keys qualify for AAL3.
Account recovery and help-desk resets must be at least as strong as the login they replace, or attackers will use them instead.
Real attacks show the hierarchy: relayed TOTP codes (Cloudflare 2022, stopped by FIDO2 keys), push fatigue (Uber 2022), and synced codes plus voice phishing (Retool 2023).
glossary: AAGUID
Authenticator Attestation GUID: an identifier of the authenticator model, reported in WebAuthn registration.
Attestation
An optional signed statement from an authenticator at registration about what kind of device it is.
Authenticator
The device or software holding WebAuthn keys: a security key, a phone, a laptop's platform authenticator, a password manager.
Base32
An encoding using the letters A-Z and digits 2-7, used for TOTP secrets because it is easy to type without confusing characters.
Conditional mediation
WebAuthn's autofill-style UI, where available passkeys appear in the username field's suggestions.
CTAP
Client to Authenticator Protocol: how a browser or OS talks to an external authenticator such as a USB security key.
Discoverable credential
A WebAuthn credential stored on the authenticator with the user's handle, so it can be used without first typing a username; passkeys are discoverable.
Dynamic truncation
The HOTP step that uses the last 4 bits of the HMAC as an offset to pick 4 bytes and turn them into a short number.
FIDO2
The FIDO Alliance's standards for passwordless login: W3C WebAuthn in the browser plus CTAP between the browser and external authenticators.
HOTP
HMAC-based one-time password (RFC 4226): a code from a shared secret and a counter.
MFA fatigue
Flooding a user with push approval requests until they accept one out of annoyance or confusion.
Number matching
A push-MFA defence where the login screen shows a number the user must enter or pick in the app, tying the approval to the session they started.
Origin binding
Including the website's origin in what the authenticator signs, so a signature made for a phishing site is useless at the real one.
OTP
One-time password: a code valid for a single use or a short window.
Passkey
A FIDO/WebAuthn discoverable credential used instead of a password, often synced across a user's devices by their platform.
Phishing-resistant
An authenticator whose output can't be relayed by a fake site to the real one, because it is bound to the origin or the channel.
Platform authenticator
An authenticator built into the device, such as Windows Hello, Touch ID or Android's screen lock.
Push MFA
A second factor where an app on the user's phone receives a notification and the user approves the login.
Recovery codes
Single-use backup codes issued at MFA enrolment for when the primary factor is lost.
Relying party ID (RP ID)
The domain a WebAuthn credential is scoped to, such as example.com; the authenticator refuses to use it for other domains.
Roaming authenticator
An external authenticator such as a USB or NFC security key that works with many devices.
SIM swap
Fraudulently moving a victim's phone number to a SIM card the attacker controls, to receive their SMS codes and calls.
TOTP
Time-based one-time password (RFC 6238): HOTP with the counter replaced by the current 30-second time step.
User verification (UV)
A WebAuthn flag meaning the authenticator checked the user locally with a PIN or biometric, not just presence.
WebAuthn
W3C Web Authentication: the browser API for creating and using public-key credentials scoped to a site.
drill:
Decide: MFA strategy for a fintech with consumers, support agents and engineers

A payments app has 2 million consumers (SMS MFA at login today), 300 support agents who can change customers' phone numbers and emails, and 80 engineers with production access (TOTP). A phishing campaign is targeting support agents, and SIM-swap fraud against consumers is rising. Design the next 6 months, naming what you'd accept for each group and why.

Answer

Engineers (highest blast radius). Two FIDO2 hardware keys each, enforced at the IdP for SSO and production access, all other methods removed for them; device-bound, so AAL3-capable. Enrolment of a new key requires an existing key or in-person verification. Done in the first month.

Support agents (targeted now, and they control recovery). Hardware keys or device-bound platform passkeys, no codes. Their tools are a recovery path for 2 million accounts, so: changing a customer's phone or email requires a second agent's approval or the customer's confirmation via an existing passkey; every change notifies the old channel; changes trigger a cooling-off period before payouts. Log and review agent actions.

Consumers. Offer synced passkeys with conditional UI and prompt after each SMS login; target passkeys as default for new devices. For users still on SMS: block payouts for 24-72 hours after a phone-number change or new-device login, detect SIM swaps (carrier APIs where available, or sudden number-change signals), and require step-up via an existing passkey for adding payees. Keep TOTP as an option. Recovery: recovery codes at enrolment, waiting periods with notifications, and no agent override without strong verification.

Measure. Phishing-resistant share of logins per group (engineers and agents 100% by month 2), consumer passkey adoption, SIM-swap-related fraud losses, agent-initiated account changes per day and their reversal rate.
qa: E
What makes something multi-factor, and what are the factor categories?

Requiring evidence from at least two different categories: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a phone app, a security key, a device's TPM) and something you are (a biometric). Two passwords are still one factor. A passkey on a phone unlocked with a fingerprint is multi-factor on its own: possession of the device's key plus a local biometric or PIN check.
E
How is a TOTP code computed?

Both sides share a secret, usually 20 random bytes shown to the user as a base32 QR code. Each side computes T = floor(Unix time / 30), packs T as an 8-byte big-endian integer, computes HMAC-SHA1(secret, T), takes the low 4 bits of the last byte as an offset, reads 4 bytes from that offset, clears the top bit, and takes the number modulo 10^6 for six digits. The server accepts the code for the current step and usually one step either side for clock drift.
Follow-up: what does the server have to store? — The shared secret itself, encrypted, plus the last accepted time step so a code can't be reused within its window.
E
Why is SMS considered a weak second factor?

The code travels through the phone network and is controlled by the carrier's account systems. Attackers SIM-swap — persuade or bribe a carrier to move the number to their SIM — or port the number, and then receive every code. SS7 network weaknesses and phone malware can intercept messages too. And like any code, it can be typed into a phishing page. It still blocks most credential stuffing, which is why it's better than nothing, but NIST classifies it as restricted.
M
Explain how a real-time phishing proxy defeats TOTP, and why WebAuthn doesn't fall to it.

The phishing page collects the username and password, relays them instantly to the real site, which asks for a code; the page asks the victim for the code too and relays it within its 30-second window; the attacker receives the session cookie. Nothing in a TOTP code says which site it was typed into. With WebAuthn, the browser puts the actual origin into the signed client data, and the authenticator only uses credentials whose RP ID matches the site's domain — on the phishing domain it won't even find the real site's credential. Even a proxied challenge produces a signature over the wrong origin, which the real server rejects.
Follow-up: what did Cloudflare see in 2022? — 76 employees received phishing texts and three entered credentials, but every employee used FIDO2 security keys, so the relayed logins failed.
M
What is MFA fatigue and how do you mitigate it?

The attacker has the password and triggers push approvals repeatedly, at odd hours, until the user taps Approve — Uber's September 2022 breach began this way, with a contractor accepting a request after repeated prompts. Mitigations: number matching (the login screen shows a number the user must enter in the app), showing location and app context in the prompt, rate-limiting pushes and alerting on bursts, an easy 'this wasn't me' that locks the login and alerts security, and moving high-risk users to phishing-resistant authenticators.
M
Walk through a WebAuthn login (assertion).

The server generates a random challenge and sends it with its RP ID and, optionally, a list of allowed credential IDs. The browser calls navigator.credentials.get(); the authenticator finds a credential for that RP ID, checks user presence and optionally verifies the user with a PIN or biometric, and signs authenticatorData (SHA-256 of the RP ID, flags, signature counter) concatenated with SHA-256 of clientDataJSON (type webauthn.get, the challenge, the origin). The server checks the challenge is the one it issued and unexpired, the origin is its own, the RP ID hash matches, the flags meet policy (UP, and UV if required), and verifies the signature with the public key stored at registration.
Follow-up: what does the server store per credential? — Credential ID, public key, signature counter, transports, backup flags and the user handle; never a secret.
M
Synced passkeys vs device-bound security keys: trade-offs?

Synced passkeys (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, third-party managers) copy the private key across the user's devices through an end-to-end encrypted sync, so losing a phone doesn't lose the account — great for consumer adoption and recovery. But the key is exportable to the sync fabric, so its security includes the user's cloud account, and NIST SP 800-63B-4 says syncable authenticators shall not be used at AAL3. Device-bound keys (a hardware security key, or a non-synced platform key) never leave the device: strongest assurance, but you need a second key or another recovery method. Typical policy: synced passkeys for customers, hardware keys for administrators and production access.
M
How should account recovery work when a user loses their second factor?

Recovery must be at least as strong as the login it replaces, or attackers use it instead. Offer recovery codes at enrolment (single-use, stored hashed), encourage registering two authenticators, and allow recovery through another registered factor. Where none is available, use a slower process: identity re-verification, a waiting period (for example 24-72 hours) with notifications to every registered channel so the real owner can cancel, and no immediate access to sensitive actions afterwards. Help-desk resets need scripts that never accept knowledge anyone could find or a voice that could be faked — Retool's 2023 breach used a deepfaked voice call impersonating IT.
H
Retool's 2023 breach is described as 'MFA that wasn't MFA'. Explain.

Attackers SMS-phished an employee, then called them with a deepfaked voice of an IT staff member and obtained an MFA code, then added their own device to the employee's Okta account. Retool's write-up says the employee's codes were in Google Authenticator with Google's then-new cloud sync, so compromising the employee's Google account exposed every TOTP seed — the second factor lived in the same account as the first. 27 cloud customers' accounts were accessed. The structural point: a 'something you have' factor stops being one when its secret is synced to an account protected by 'something you know', and any code-based factor can be talked out of a person. Retool recommended FIDO2 hardware keys and human verification for sensitive actions.
H
Compute the probability of guessing a 6-digit TOTP with and without rate limits.

With a ±1 step window the server accepts 3 codes at any moment, so each random guess succeeds with probability 3/10^6 = 3 × 10^-6. NIST caps consecutive failures at 100: 100 guesses give about 3 × 10^-4, 0.03%. Without limits, an attacker making 10 guesses per second for a day makes 864,000 guesses, so the chance of at least one success is 1 − (1 − 3×10^-6)^864000 ≈ 1 − e^-2.59 ≈ 92%. Six digits are only safe because the server limits attempts — which is why OTP endpoints need rate limits per account, not just per IP.
Follow-up: why do servers accept adjacent windows at all? — Phone clocks drift and users take seconds to type; accepting ±1 step trades a 3× larger guess space for usability.
H
Roll out phishing-resistant MFA to 5,000 employees. Plan it.

Start with the highest-risk groups — admins, engineers with production access, finance, help desk — on two hardware security keys each, enforced in the IdP by policy so password-plus-code no longer works for them. Enable platform passkeys for everyone else, keep TOTP as a temporary fallback with a sunset date, and remove SMS. Harden the edges: require a key for adding or removing authenticators, re-verify identity in person or by video plus manager approval for help-desk resets, monitor enrolment of new authenticators and logins without phishing-resistant methods. Measure coverage weekly, and run phishing simulations to confirm the fallback paths are gone. Cloudflare's 2022 experience is the business case: three employees fell for a convincing phish and nothing happened.
H
Why are passkeys resistant to server-side database breaches, and what still needs protecting?

The server stores only public keys and credential IDs, so a database dump gives the attacker nothing to log in with or crack — there's no shared secret like a password hash or a TOTP seed. What still needs protecting: the session issued after login (au3), recovery and enrolment flows (an attacker who can add their own passkey owns the account), the challenge generation and verification logic (reused or predictable challenges, origin checks skipped), and the integrity of the stored public keys — an attacker with write access to the credentials table could insert their own key. So protect writes to that table as carefully as you'd protect password changes.

t: Authorisation models: ACLs, RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC and Zanzibar, policy engines (OPA, Cedar) and where to enforce
sum: How systems decide "may this subject do this action on this resource?": access control lists, role-based access with role explosion, attribute-based policies, relationship-based access and Google's Zanzibar (tuples, userset rewrites, the new-enemy problem and zookies), the same "can Alice edit doc 42?" question answered by RBAC and by ReBAC step by step, policy engines OPA and Cedar with real policies, and the trade-offs of centralised versus in-service enforcement.
prereq: au1
Authorisation decides on subject, action and resource; it has function, object and property levels; PEPs enforce and PDPs decide; deny by default.
swe13
Broken object-level authorisation is the top API risk; centralise decisions, scope queries by tenant, return 404 for invisible objects, and test with other users' IDs.
au4
Tokens carry identity and coarse scopes but are frozen until expiry, so volatile permissions should be looked up at decision time rather than embedded.
sc2
Gateways and service meshes sit in the request path and can run per-request checks, but only coarse ones that don't need business data.
why:
Imagine you're building a document editor. On day one, authorisation is one line: if doc.owner_id == user.id. Then customers ask to share a document with a colleague, so you add a shared_with list. Then they want to share with a whole team, so you add groups. Then folders, and documents should inherit a folder's sharing. Then "anyone in my company with the link can view". Then enterprise admins want "nobody may share outside the company", and legal wants "documents labelled confidential can't be downloaded by contractors". Then a support engineer needs to see a customer's document for an hour to debug it, with the customer's permission. Each rule is reasonable. Two years later, the authorisation logic is spread across forty handlers, no two of which agree about inheritance, and the security team can't answer the simplest audit question: "who can see this document, and why?"

Google faced this across Drive, Docs, Photos, Calendar, YouTube and Cloud, and in 2019 published how it solved it: Zanzibar, a single authorisation system holding trillions of access-control entries and answering millions of checks per second with 95th-percentile latency under 10 milliseconds and better than 99.999% availability over three years. Its central idea — represent permissions as relationships in a graph and derive access by following them — has since spawned a family of open-source systems.

Not every product needs Zanzibar. Many need roles and an ownership check; some need attribute rules; most large ones end up combining models. au1 established that authorisation is the decision "may this subject do this action on this resource?", made on every request at the object level. This topic is about how to make that decision well at scale: the four classic models (ACLs, RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC) and what each is good and bad at; the same question — "can Alice edit doc 42?" — answered by RBAC and by ReBAC step by step; how Zanzibar works, including the consistency problem it names the "new enemy"; policy engines (OPA and Cedar) that move rules out of application code; and where enforcement should live in a distributed system. This app's own authorisation, two roles and ownership scoping, serves as the small baseline.
primer:
Four ways to run a building's doors

Picture four ways to decide who may enter which room in an office building.

A list on every door: room 401 has a sheet saying "Alice, Bob, Carol". That's an access control list (ACL). Very direct: to know who can enter 401, read its sheet. Painful when Alice changes teams and you must find every sheet with her name.

Badges by job: everyone gets a badge type — engineer, finance, visitor — and each door accepts certain types. That's role-based access control (RBAC). Easy to manage and audit ("what can engineers open?"), but it can't express "Alice may enter Bob's office while Bob is on holiday" without inventing a new badge type, and soon there are hundreds of badge types.

A guard who checks a rulebook: "finance staff may enter finance rooms during business hours if their security training is current". The guard looks at facts about you, the room and the time. That's attribute-based access control (ABAC). Flexible, but the guard is only as good as the facts (is training status up to date?) and the rulebook can become unreadable.

Following relationships: "you may enter a room if you're a member of a team that owns the floor it's on". To decide, the guard follows links: room → floor → owning team → members. That's relationship-based access control (ReBAC). It models how organisations actually share things — through ownership, membership and containment — and one change (Alice leaves the team) correctly updates access to everything reached through that link.

The analogy's limit: in software, decisions happen millions of times a second, across many services, on data that changes constantly. That turns the choice of model into a systems problem — where the data lives, how fresh it is, how fast a check runs — as much as a modelling one.

What every model must get right

Whichever model you pick, four properties decide whether it works in production. Correctness: the rules say what the business means, including the awkward cases (a user in two teams, a document moved between folders, a contractor who becomes an employee). Freshness: when someone loses access, how many seconds until every service agrees? Speed: a check runs on nearly every request, so it has a latency budget of a few milliseconds at most. Explainability: for any decision, someone can say why — which role, attribute or relationship produced it — because auditors, customers and your own on-call engineers will ask. Models trade these off differently: ACLs are explainable and fresh but awkward to manage; roles are fast and explainable but coarse; attributes are flexible but hard to explain; relationship graphs are expressive and explainable but need careful engineering for speed and freshness.

If you stop here: roles for coarse job functions, relationships for sharing and hierarchy, attributes for context like time, location and labels — and in every case, default deny, one place where the rules live, and enforcement where the object is loaded.
body:
1. The vocabulary of a decision

Every authorisation decision has the same inputs: a subject (who is asking — a user, a service, an agent, as au1 described), an action (edit, view, delete, export), a resource (document 42, invoice 1043, the admin panel) and context (time, IP address, whether MFA was used recently, the tenant). Its output is allow or deny. Architecture adds three roles, standardised in ABAC literature such as NIST SP 800-162: the policy enforcement point (PEP), which intercepts the request and enforces the result; the policy decision point (PDP), which computes it; and the policy information point (PIP), which supplies facts the PDP needs — group memberships, document owners, labels.

Two rules apply to every model. Default deny: if no rule grants access, the answer is no, and errors or missing data lead to no. Least privilege: grant the minimum for the minimum time. The models differ in how they express grants.

2. Access control lists

An ACL attaches to each resource a list of entries (principal, permissions). File systems are the classic example: a POSIX file has owner, group and other permissions, and extended ACLs add named users and groups; cloud storage buckets and objects have ACLs too. Checking is a lookup: read the resource's ACL, see if the subject (or a group they're in) has the action.

ACLs are excellent for per-object sharing ("share this one file with Bob"), and the question "who can access this resource?" is answered by reading one list. They're weak at the reverse question — "what can Bob access?" means scanning every ACL — and at change: when Bob leaves the company, every ACL mentioning him must be found. Groups in ACL entries help, but inheritance (a folder's ACL applying to its contents) must be implemented by copying or by walking parents, and copying goes stale. Cloud providers' experience is telling: AWS now recommends disabling S3 object ACLs and using policies instead, because per-object ACLs made it too easy to make individual objects public unnoticed.

3. Role-based access control

RBAC inserts roles between users and permissions: permissions are granted to roles (editor → document.edit, document.view), users are assigned roles. NIST's RBAC model adds role hierarchies (admin inherits editor) and constraints such as separation of duties (the person who creates a supplier can't also approve payments to it).

RBAC's strengths are management and audit. "What can editors do?" and "who are the admins?" are single queries. Onboarding is assigning a role that matches a job. Most products have some RBAC, even if it's two roles. This app has exactly that: signed-in users and administrators, where "administrator" is decided by the email being in the ADMIN_EMAILS environment setting, re-evaluated on every request by admin_required.

Its weakness is that roles don't know about objects. "Editor" means editor of everything the role covers. In multi-tenant products that's fixed by scoping roles to a tenant (Alice is an editor in Acme), which is still coarse. When products need per-object exceptions — this one project, this one document, this customer's records — teams create roles for them, and you get role explosion: thousands of roles that nobody can audit. Role explosion is the clearest signal that some decisions belong to attributes or relationships.

4. Attribute-based access control

ABAC computes decisions from attributes using policies. Attributes come from the subject (department, clearance, employment type), the resource (owner, classification label, region), the action, and the environment (time, network, device posture, how recently MFA was used). A policy might read: "Allow view if subject.department == resource.department and resource.label != 'restricted', or if the subject is the resource's owner; deny all download by contractors from unmanaged devices."

ABAC handles context that roles can't — time windows, data residency, device trust, step-up freshness — and avoids role explosion by expressing rules over properties. Its costs: decisions depend on attributes being correct and fresh (a stale department attribute grants the wrong access); policies can become hard to read, so reasoning about "who can see this?" requires evaluating policies against every user; and a missing attribute must evaluate to deny, not to an accidental allow. Good ABAC systems treat policies as code: versioned, reviewed, unit-tested and analysed.

5. Relationship-based access control

ReBAC represents facts as relationships — user is member of group, group is editor of folder, folder is parent of document — and derives permissions by following them. It fits collaborative products, where access spreads through sharing, groups and containment, and it makes changes cheap: removing Alice from one group changes her access to everything reached through that group, without touching any document.

Google's Zanzibar is the reference design. Its data model is the relation tuple:

⟨object⟩#⟨relation⟩@⟨user⟩            doc:42#owner@user:carol
⟨object⟩#⟨relation⟩@⟨object#relation⟩   folder:7#editor@group:design#member

The second form uses a userset — "everyone who is a member of group:design" — as the subject, which is how groups and nesting work. Each namespace (document, folder, group) has a configuration with userset rewrites that define relations in terms of others:

document:
  owner   = this
  editor  = this ∪ owner ∪ (parent → editor)     # direct editors, owners, and the parent folder's editors
  viewer  = this ∪ editor ∪ (parent → viewer)
folder:
  editor  = this ∪ (parent → editor)
group:
  member  = this

this means directly stored tuples; owner inside editor means "owners are also editors" (a computed userset); parent → editor means "follow this object's parent tuple and take that object's editors" (Zanzibar calls it tuple-to-userset). Services ask four kinds of question: Check (does user U have relation R on object O?), Read (list tuples), Expand (show the full tree of who has R on O) and Write; a Watch API streams changes for building indexes.

6. Worked example: "can Alice edit doc 42?"

The setup: tenant Acme. Doc 42 lives in folder 7, a design team folder. Alice is a designer. Bob is a salesperson who's an editor in Acme generally. Carol owns doc 42.

With RBAC. The data:

role_permissions: editor → {document.view, document.edit}; viewer → {document.view}
user_roles:       (alice, acme) → editor;  (bob, acme) → editor;  (dave, acme) → viewer
documents:        42 → tenant acme

Check: Alice's roles in doc 42's tenant (Acme) = {editor}; editor's permissions include document.edit; allow. One lookup of Alice's roles, one of the role's permissions, one of the document's tenant. Now the same check for Bob: also allow — and for every other document in Acme. RBAC can't say "design documents are editable by designers only" without roles like design-editor, and can't say "Carol shared this one document with Dave as editor" without a per-document exception, which is exactly how role explosion begins.

With ReBAC. The tuples:

doc:42#owner@user:carol
doc:42#parent@folder:7
folder:7#editor@group:design#member
group:design#member@user:alice
group:sales#member@user:bob

Check doc:42#editor@user:alice, following the rewrite editor = this ∪ owner ∪ (parent → editor):

  1. this: is there a tuple doc:42#editor@user:alice? Read 1 — no.
  2. owner: is Alice the owner? The owner tuple names Carol (same read) — no.
  3. parent → editor: read doc 42's parent tuples (read 2) — folder:7. Now check folder:7#editor@user:alice: its this tuples (read 3) include the userset group:design#member. Check group:design#member@user:alice (read 4) — yes.
  4. Result: allow, with the path doc:42 → parent folder:7 → editor group:design → member alice.

The same check for Bob fails at step 3 (Bob is in sales, not design). If Carol shares doc 42 with Dave as editor, that's one new tuple doc:42#editor@user:dave, and step 1 succeeds for Dave on doc 42 only. If Alice leaves the design team, one tuple is deleted and every document reached through folder 7 or any other design-team grant is no longer editable by her. And "why can Alice edit this?" has a precise answer: the path.

7. Zanzibar's consistency problem: the new enemy

Authorisation data changes, and checks read replicas and caches. Zanzibar's paper names the danger the new enemy problem and gives two examples. First: Alice removes Bob from a folder's ACL, then adds a new confidential document to it; if a check for Bob reads a stale snapshot taken before the removal while the document is already visible, Bob sees content added after he was removed. Second: Alice removes Bob, then asks Charlie to add new content; the ordering between different users' actions must also be respected.

Zanzibar solves it with Google's Spanner database, whose TrueTime clocks give a global ordering of commits, and with zookies: opaque tokens encoding a timestamp. When a client changes content (say, saves a new version of doc 42), it asks Zanzibar for a zookie for that object and stores it with the content version. Later checks of that content pass the zookie, and Zanzibar evaluates them at a snapshot at least as fresh as the zookie — so any ACL change committed before the content change is visible. Checks without a fresh-content requirement can use older snapshots, which are served from caches and are much faster. That split — fresh enough for correctness, otherwise as stale as is fast — is how Zanzibar reaches sub-10 ms p95 at its scale.

Two other engineering pieces from the paper matter in interviews. Deeply nested groups make checks slow (group of groups of groups), so Zanzibar maintains Leopard, an index that denormalises nested group membership into flat sets for fast intersection. And popular objects create hot spots, handled by request deduplication and caching tuned per namespace.

8. Policy engines: OPA and Cedar

Whatever the model, writing rules as scattered if statements is how inconsistency starts. Policy engines move rules into a dedicated language that's versioned, tested and evaluated by one engine.

Open Policy Agent (OPA), a graduated CNCF project, evaluates policies written in Rego, a Datalog-inspired language, against JSON input (the request) and data (loaded facts). The doc-edit rule as Rego (OPA 1.0 syntax):

package docs.authz

default allow := false

allow if {
    input.action == "edit"
    some role in data.user_roles[input.tenant][input.user]
    "document.edit" in data.role_permissions[role]
    data.documents[input.resource].tenant == input.tenant
}

allow if {
    input.action in {"view", "edit"}
    data.documents[input.resource].owner == input.user
}

OPA runs as a library, a sidecar next to each service, or a central service; it's popular for infrastructure policy too (Kubernetes admission control, Terraform plan checks), because anything that can be expressed as JSON can be checked.

Cedar, open-sourced by AWS in 2023 and used by Amazon Verified Permissions, is a language designed specifically for application authorisation. Policies are permit or forbid over typed principals, actions and resources, with conditions:

permit (
    principal,
    action == Action::"edit",
    resource is Document
) when { principal in resource.folder.editors };

forbid (
    principal,
    action == Action::"download",
    resource is Document
) when { resource.label == "confidential" && principal.employment == "contractor" };

Cedar's semantics are deliberately simple: with no matching permit, the result is deny; any matching forbid overrides every permit. Entities can have parents (principal in group), so it can express some relationship logic, and a schema lets tools validate policies and analyse them — for example, prove that no policy lets a guest delete. Cedar's documentation describes it as designed for verification, and AWS has published work on formally verifying the engine.

The engines separate policy from data. The PDP still needs facts — Alice's roles, doc 42's folder, folder 7's editors — from a PIP. Getting fresh facts to the engine is the hard part, which is why ReBAC systems store relationships themselves and why OPA deployments often have data-synchronisation pipelines.

9. Where to enforce

Enforcement and decision are separate choices. Enforcement (the PEP) must live where the object and action are known precisely: inside the service, around every code path that touches data — HTTP handlers, but also batch jobs, exports, admin tools, message consumers. The gateway (sc2) can enforce coarse rules (is there a token, is this client allowed on this route, required scopes) but not object-level ones.

Decision placement has three common shapes:

PDP placementLatencyFreshness of dataConsistency of rulesFailure mode
In-process library (policies + data pushed in)microsecondsas fresh as the last syncsame policy bundle everywherestale data
Sidecar (OPA next to each service)sub-millisecondas fresh as the last synccentral policy distributionstale data; sidecar down
Central service (Zanzibar-style)a network hop, cachedfresh (consistency tokens)single source of truthcritical dependency; outage blocks requests

Large systems mix them: tenant and scope checks at the gateway, relationship checks against a central ReBAC service, attribute rules (time, device, labels) in a local engine, and data filters in queries. Whatever the mix, deny by default when the PDP is unavailable, and make "this endpoint's authorisation" something a reviewer can find in one place.
deep:
Authorisation for lists is a query problem

Per-object checks answer "may Alice see doc 42?". Products constantly ask a different question: "show Alice the documents she can see, sorted by date, page 3". Checking each candidate after fetching works for tiny sets and fails at scale: you fetch 1,000 documents to show 20, pagination shifts unpredictably, and counts leak. Three patterns exist. Filter in the database when the rule is simple (tenant plus owner plus a shares table) — this is how the Prep Console's WHERE user_id = ? works. Ask the authorisation system for the accessible set ("lookup resources") and intersect it with the query — feasible when the set is small or the system maintains a reverse index. Or index coarse permission data with the content (tenant ID, ACL group IDs on each search document), filter in the search engine, and post-check only the top results exactly. The last is the standard design for enterprise search and RAG (hd2, au12), with the subtle requirement that the index's permission data is updated as fast as permissions change.

Caching decisions without breaking revocation

Authorisation checks are hot: every request makes one or more. Caching is essential and dangerous. Cache keys must include everything the decision depended on (subject, action, resource, relevant context), and TTLs bound how long a revoked permission keeps working. Zanzibar's design is instructive: it caches aggressively at snapshot timestamps, and zookies decide when a cached snapshot is too old for a given request. Without consistency tokens, the practical approach is short TTLs (seconds), explicit invalidation on permission writes for the affected subjects or objects, and a bypass for sensitive actions. Measure the revocation latency you actually achieve.

Combining models

Real policies are hybrids. Google Drive's sharing is ReBAC, but a Workspace admin's "no external sharing" is an attribute policy layered on top, and some actions are reserved to roles (domain admins). A clean way to combine them is layering with explicit precedence: forbid-style guardrails (tenant boundaries, legal holds, data residency) evaluated first and able to override; then relationship and role grants; then default deny. Cedar's "forbid overrides permit" encodes exactly that precedence. The design mistake to avoid is two systems that can each independently grant access, so that turning a permission off in one leaves it on in the other.

Explaining and auditing decisions

"Who can access this, and why?" is a question regulators, customers and incident responders ask. ACLs answer it directly; RBAC answers via role membership; ReBAC answers via Expand (the tree of usersets) and per-check paths; ABAC is hardest, because you must evaluate policies against every subject. Build explanation in: return the matching policy or the relationship path with each decision (at least in logs), and offer an "access review" feature that lists principals and the reason for each. Periodic access reviews — managers confirming their reports' access — are a compliance requirement in many industries and only work if the system can enumerate access.

Policy as code, tested like code

Policies deserve the same engineering discipline as application code: version control, code review, unit tests (OPA has a built-in test runner; Cedar has validation against a schema), and regression tests built from real decisions. A powerful technique when migrating is shadow evaluation: run the new engine alongside existing checks, log disagreements, and investigate each — disagreements are frequently real bugs in the old code. Another is differential testing of policy changes: evaluate the old and new policy sets against a sample of recent requests and review every changed decision before deploying.

Negative permissions and exclusions

Pure grant-based models struggle with "everyone in engineering except interns" or "all of the folder except this one file". ReBAC systems add exclusion and intersection operators to their rewrites (Zanzibar's configs support union, intersection and exclusion of usersets), and Cedar has forbid. Use them sparingly: exclusions make reasoning harder, because adding a user to a group can now remove access elsewhere, and they interact badly with caches that assume permissions only grow when tuples are added.

Authorisation for machines and agents

Services and agents are principals too (au1, au10). Service authorisation is often expressed as "service A may call method M of service B" — function-level rules, natural to enforce in a service mesh with workload identity. Agents acting for users need two decisions at once: may this user do this, and may this agent do this on the user's behalf? ReBAC handles that elegantly — the agent's permissions can be modelled as a relation derived from the user's, intersected with what the delegation allows — and au12 builds on it.
prod:
Failure modes

Forgotten enforcement points. The web handler checks, the CSV export job doesn't; the REST API checks, the GraphQL resolver for a nested field doesn't. Most IDOR findings are here. Mitigate with framework-level enforcement (a decorator or middleware every handler must declare), and tests that call every route with a second tenant's IDs.

Stale permission data. A user removed from a group keeps access because a cache, a token or a replicated policy bundle hasn't updated. Symptoms surface as customer complaints after offboarding. Measure revocation latency end to end.

PDP outages. A central authorisation service on every request's path is critical infrastructure; when it's slow, everything is slow. Budget its latency (single-digit milliseconds p99), cache, run it multi-region, and decide per action whether to fail closed or serve a bounded-age cached decision.

Policy drift. Two services enforce "editors can delete" differently because each copied the rule. Centralise rules in one policy repository even if evaluation is distributed.

Over-broad admin roles. Support and operations roles accumulate permissions until they can read every customer's data. Use just-in-time elevation with approval and expiry, and log every use.

Metrics and signals

Decisions per second and PDP latency (p50/p99) per service; deny rate per endpoint and per subject (spikes suggest probing or a broken deployment); cross-tenant access attempts (should be zero); cache hit rate and revocation latency; number of roles and of users per role (role explosion shows up as a long tail of single-user roles); count of standing privileged grants vs just-in-time grants.

The Zanzibar paper as a production case

The paper's production numbers are worth knowing precisely: trillions of ACLs, millions of authorisation requests per second, 95th-percentile latency under 10 milliseconds, and availability above 99.999% over three years, serving Calendar, Cloud, Drive, Maps, Photos, YouTube and other Google services. Its engineering lessons generalise: separate consistency needs (fresh for content-protecting checks, cached otherwise); flatten nested groups into an index; deduplicate concurrent identical checks; and give every client the same semantics so sharing behaves the same across products. Open-source systems inspired by it — OpenFGA, SpiceDB and others — implement the tuple model and modelling language; whether to adopt one is a question of whether your product's permissions are really a graph (sharing, groups, hierarchy) or mostly roles plus ownership.

Testing authorisation

Authorisation bugs are silent, so tests carry more weight than usual. Keep a matrix test per resource type: for each role or relationship (owner, editor, viewer, other user in the tenant, user in another tenant, anonymous), assert the expected result for each action. Generate it from the policy where possible, so a policy change shows up as a reviewed diff in the expected matrix. Add property-style tests for invariants such as "no request where the resource's tenant differs from the caller's tenant is ever allowed", run against random IDs.

Right-sizing

The Prep Console is the other end of the spectrum: each user's data is private, there's no sharing, and two roles suffice. Its authorisation is a decorator per route plus owner-scoped queries, and that's the right amount. The senior skill is recognising which shape you're in and when you're about to cross into the next — usually the day someone asks for sharing.
myths: RBAC is enough for any application.

Roles answer 'what kind of user is this?' well and 'may this user touch this particular object?' badly. Sharing a single document with one outside person, folder inheritance, or 'managers can see their reports' records' all need per-object facts. Teams that force them into roles end up with thousands of roles like editor-doc-4471 — role explosion — which nobody can audit.
Put the user's permissions in the JWT and you never need a lookup.

Tokens are frozen until expiry and limited in size. Coarse, stable facts (tenant, a few roles) fit; per-object grants don't — a user with access to 20,000 documents can't carry them in a header, and a revoked share keeps working until the token expires. Look up fine-grained permissions at decision time, with short caching.
A central authorisation service means you don't need checks in services.

A central PDP decides, but each service is still the PEP that must ask, with the right resource and action, on every path — including batch jobs, exports and admin endpoints. And the service still filters lists and fields. Centralisation fixes inconsistency of rules, not forgotten calls.
ABAC is more secure than RBAC because it's more expressive.

Expressiveness cuts both ways: complex attribute policies are harder to read, test and audit, depend on attributes being correct and fresh, and can fail open if an attribute is missing. The more secure model is the one whose decisions your team can predict and review.
Eventually consistent permission checks are fine.

Zanzibar's paper calls the failure the 'new enemy' problem: remove Bob from a folder, then add a secret document, and a stale check may show Bob the new document. Permission systems need at least a guarantee that a check sees all changes up to the content version being accessed — which is what Zanzibar's zookies provide.
lab:
Goal: build a tiny RBAC checker and a Zanzibar-style ReBAC checker in Python 3.12 (standard library only) and compare their answers. About 15 minutes.

  1. RBAC. Dicts: role_perms = {"editor": {"doc.view", "doc.edit"}, "viewer": {"doc.view"}}, user_roles = {("alice", "acme"): {"editor"}, ("bob", "acme"): {"editor"}, ("dave", "acme"): {"viewer"}}, docs = {42: "acme"}. Write rbac_check(user, perm, doc). Check Alice and Bob for doc.edit on 42.
  2. Tuples. A set of 3-tuples (object, relation, subject) where subject is "user:alice" or a userset "group:design#member". Load the five tuples from the body.
  3. Rewrites. A dict per namespace, e.g. {"document": {"editor": ["this", ("computed", "owner"), ("parent", "editor")]}}.
  4. Check. Write recursive check(obj, rel, user, seen) handling this (direct tuples, expanding usersets by calling check on them), computed relations and parent traversal; use seen to stop cycles. Return the path as a list.
  5. Compare. Alice and Bob on doc 42; then add doc:42#editor@user:dave and check Dave; then remove Alice from design and re-check.
  6. New enemy. Give each tuple a write version. Implement check_at(version) that ignores tuples written after it and honours deletes up to it. Remove Bob from a folder at version 10, add doc 99 at version 11, and check Bob on doc 99 at version 9 (stale) and at version 11 (zookie).

What to look for: RBAC allows Bob, ReBAC denies him; Dave's access appears for one document only; removing one membership tuple changes Alice's answer everywhere. The printed path explains each allow. In step 6 the stale snapshot wrongly allows Bob — the new enemy problem — and the zookie-fresh check denies him.
recap: An access control list attaches the list of who may do what to each resource; simple, per-object, and hard to manage at scale.
RBAC grants permissions to roles and roles to users, which is easy to audit but coarse, and explodes when per-object exceptions are encoded as roles.
ABAC evaluates policies over attributes of the subject, resource, action and environment, which is expressive but depends on correct, fresh attributes and readable policies.

ReBAC derives permissions from a graph of relationships (owner of, member of, parent of), which models sharing, groups and inheritance naturally; Google's Zanzibar stores trillions of such tuples and answers millions of checks per second at under 10 ms p95.
Zanzibar solves the new-enemy problem with zookies: consistency tokens that make a check at least as fresh as the content version it protects.
Policy engines like OPA (Rego) and Cedar separate policy from code, are default-deny, and can be tested and analysed; Cedar's forbid always overrides permit.
Enforcement must happen where the object is known — usually in the service — while decisions can be local libraries, sidecars or a central service, trading latency and freshness against consistency.
List endpoints and search need authorisation as filters, not just per-object checks, which is where ReBAC indexes and database filters matter.
glossary: ABAC
Attribute-based access control: decisions computed by policies over attributes of the subject, resource, action and environment.
ACL
Access control list: a list attached to a resource naming which principals may perform which actions on it.
Cedar
An open-source policy language and engine from AWS with permit/forbid policies over principals, actions, resources and context.
Check
