In Zanzibar-style systems, the API call asking whether a user has a relation to an object.
CNCF
Cloud Native Computing Foundation: the open-source foundation hosting Kubernetes, OPA and related projects.
Default deny
If no rule grants access, the answer is no.
Least privilege
Granting only the permissions needed, for only as long as needed.
Leopard
Zanzibar's index that flattens nested group membership so checks through deep group hierarchies stay fast.
New enemy problem
A consistency bug where a permission check uses stale data and grants a removed user access to content added after their removal.
OPA
Open Policy Agent: a CNCF policy engine that evaluates Rego policies against JSON input and data.
PDP
Policy decision point: computes allow or deny.
PEP
Policy enforcement point: intercepts the request and enforces the PDP's decision.
PIP
Policy information point: a source of attributes or relationships the PDP needs, such as a user directory or document database.
RBAC
Role-based access control: permissions are granted to roles, and users are assigned roles.
ReBAC
Relationship-based access control: permissions follow from relationships between objects and subjects in a graph.
Rego
OPA's declarative policy language, inspired by Datalog.
Relation tuple
Zanzibar's unit of data: object#relation@subject, such as doc:42#editor@user:alice.
Role explosion
The growth of roles into thousands of narrow variants when RBAC is used to express per-object or per-context permissions.
Separation of duties
A rule that the same person may not hold two roles (or perform two steps) whose combination enables fraud.
Shadow evaluation
Running a new policy engine alongside the existing checks, logging disagreements without enforcing, to validate a migration.
Userset
In Zanzibar, a set of users defined by a relation on an object, such as group:design#member.
Userset rewrite
A rule in a Zanzibar namespace config that computes one relation from others, such as 'viewers include editors' or 'inherit from the parent folder'.
Zookie
Zanzibar's opaque consistency token, encoding a timestamp, that makes later checks at least as fresh as a given content change.
drill:
Design: authorisation for a multi-tenant project tracker

A B2B project tracker has tenants (companies), workspaces within tenants, projects within workspaces and tasks within projects. Requirements: tenant admins manage everything in their tenant; workspace members see all projects in the workspace; projects can be private (members only); a task can be shared with an external guest; contractors may never export data; support staff can access a tenant only during an approved ticket window. Choose models, sketch the schema and policies, and say where enforcement and decision happen.

Answer

Models. ReBAC for the containment and sharing structure; RBAC-like relations for tenant admin; ABAC/forbid policies for contractors and support windows.

ReBAC schema (Zanzibar-style).

tenant:    admin = this;  member = this ∪ admin
workspace: tenant (parent); member = this ∪ (tenant → admin)
project:   workspace (parent); private (flag tuple)
           member = this ∪ (workspace → member, unless private) ∪ (workspace → tenant → admin)
task:      project (parent); guest = this
           viewer = guest ∪ (project → member);  editor = (project → member)

"Unless private" is cleanest as two relations: projects without the private flag get workspace → member; private ones don't. Guests are a direct tuple on one task.

Policies (Cedar). forbid(principal, action == Action::"export", resource) when { principal.employment == "contractor" }; and permit for support only when { context.ticket_window_active && context.ticket_tenant == resource.tenant }, with tenant boundary as a forbid: any request where the resource's tenant differs from the principal's tenant is denied unless it's the support permit.

Enforcement. Gateway: token, tenant claim, coarse scopes. Each service: PEP on every handler and job, calling a central ReBAC check service (cached, with zookies on content writes) and a local Cedar engine for the guardrails; lists filtered by workspace and project IDs from a reverse index plus tenant filter in SQL. Log every decision with the path or policy ID; build an access-review page per project.

Tests. Cross-tenant IDs return 404 on every route; contractor export is denied even for tenant admins who are contractors; support access fails outside the window; a guest sees exactly one task.
qa: E
Compare ACLs, RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC in one sentence each.

ACLs attach a list of who-can-do-what to each resource — direct and per-object, but hard to manage across many resources. RBAC gives permissions to roles and roles to users — easy to reason about and audit, but coarse. ABAC evaluates rules over attributes of user, resource and context — flexible and context-aware, but harder to read and dependent on attribute quality. ReBAC derives permissions from relationships in a graph — natural for sharing, groups and folder inheritance, at the cost of a graph store and consistency engineering.
E
How does this app (the Prep Console) authorise requests?

Two layers. Function level, two roles: any signed-in user (login_required) and administrators (admin_required), where admin means the email is listed in the ADMIN_EMAILS environment setting, rechecked on every request. Object level by ownership: every progress table is keyed by user_id and every query includes WHERE user_id = ? with the id from the session, so a user can only ever touch their own rows. It's a minimal RBAC plus owner-scoping, which fits an app where nothing is shared between users.
E
What is role explosion?

When per-object or per-context permissions are forced into RBAC, roles multiply: editor-for-project-17, viewer-of-finance-docs-in-EU, contractor-read-only-until-March. Thousands of roles become impossible to audit or reason about, and assigning the right one becomes error-prone. It's a signal you need attributes (ABAC) or relationships (ReBAC) for those decisions, with RBAC kept for coarse job functions.
M
Answer 'can Alice edit doc 42?' with RBAC, then with ReBAC.

RBAC: look up Alice's roles in tenant Acme — editor; the editor role includes the permission document.edit; doc 42 belongs to Acme; so allow. Note what that means: Alice can edit every Acme document, because roles don't know about objects. ReBAC: tuples say doc:42#parent@folder:7, folder:7#editor@group:design#member, and group:design#member@user:alice. The schema says a doc's editors are its direct editors plus its parent's editors. Check doc:42#editor@alice: no direct tuple; follow parent to folder:7; folder:7's editors include members of group:design; Alice is a member; allow. Remove Alice from design, or move doc 42 out of folder 7, and the answer changes for that document only.

Follow-up: how many reads did the ReBAC check take, and how does that scale? — Three tuple lookups here; deep nesting means more, which is why Zanzibar caches heavily and denormalises nested group membership in its Leopard index.
M
What is Zanzibar and why was it built?

Google's global authorisation system, described in a USENIX ATC 2019 paper. It stores permissions for Calendar, Cloud, Drive, Maps, Photos, YouTube and others as relation tuples (object#relation@user or @userset), with per-namespace configs that define how relations derive from each other. Services call Check, Read, Expand and Write. The paper reports trillions of ACLs, millions of authorisation requests per second, 95th-percentile latency under 10 ms and availability above 99.999% over three years. It was built so that sharing semantics are consistent across products — a document shared to a group behaves the same in Drive and in Docs embedded in Gmail — and so that consistency and scale are solved once.
M
Explain the new-enemy problem and zookies.

Two failure orders. Alice removes Bob from a folder, then adds a secret document; if the check for Bob reads a replica that hasn't seen the removal but the document is visible, Bob sees it. Or Alice removes Bob from the ACL and then asks Charlie to add content; ordering across users matters too. Zanzibar runs on Spanner, whose TrueTime gives globally meaningful timestamps. When content changes, the client asks Zanzibar for a zookie — an opaque token encoding a timestamp at least as late as the latest ACL change — and stores it with the content version. Later checks for that content pass the zookie, and Zanzibar evaluates them at a snapshot no older than that, while otherwise using older, cached snapshots for speed.
M
OPA vs Cedar: what are they and when would you use each?

Both separate policy from application code and default to deny. OPA is a general-purpose CNCF engine: policies in Rego, a Datalog-inspired language, evaluated against arbitrary JSON input and data; it's used for Kubernetes admission, API authorisation, Terraform checks — anywhere you can hand it JSON. Cedar, open-sourced by AWS in 2023, is purpose-built for application authorisation: permit and forbid policies over typed principals, actions and resources, with a schema, and forbid always overrides permit; it's designed to be analysable, so tools can prove properties like 'no policy lets a guest delete'. Choose OPA for broad infrastructure policy and existing ecosystem; Cedar for application permissions where readability and analysis matter.
M
Where should authorisation be enforced: centrally or in each service?

Separate deciding from enforcing. Enforcement has to be where the request touches the object — inside the service, on every path including background jobs — because only there are the resource and action known precisely. The decision can be an in-process library with policies pushed to it (fast, no network, but data must be replicated), a sidecar such as OPA beside each service (local latency, central policy distribution), or a central service such as a Zanzibar-style system (fresh shared data, one consistent answer, but a network hop and a critical dependency). Most large systems mix them: coarse checks at the gateway, relationship checks in a central service, attribute rules in local engines.

Follow-up: what happens when the central authorisation service is down? — Fail closed for writes and sensitive reads; for low-risk reads you may serve cached decisions with a short bound, and you must engineer the service for high availability because it's now on every request's path.
M
How do you authorise list and search endpoints?

Per-object checks after fetching don't work well: you fetch 100 results, discard 97, and pagination breaks. Options: push authorisation into the query as a filter (WHERE tenant_id = ? AND (owner_id = ? OR id IN shared_with_me)), which works when rules are simple and data is local; ask the authorisation system for the set of objects the user can access (Zanzibar-style 'lookup resources' or a reverse index) and intersect with the search; or pre-filter by coarse attributes in the search index (tenant, ACL group IDs stored on each document) and post-filter the top results with exact checks. Search over permissions is one of the hardest parts of authorisation, and the place enterprise RAG systems get wrong (au12).
H
Design authorisation for a Google Docs-like product.

Model with ReBAC: namespaces for user, group, folder and document; document relations owner, editor, commenter, viewer, parent; rewrites so viewer includes commenter includes editor includes owner, and each includes the same relation on the parent folder; groups have member with nested groups. Store tuples in a replicated store with a Check API, cache aggressively, and denormalise nested group membership for fast checks. Use zookies: when a document is edited, record the zookie; checks for that version must be at least that fresh. Link sharing becomes a tuple doc:42#viewer@anyone-with-link with a token check. Lists ('shared with me') come from a reverse index. Attributes like 'external sharing disabled for this tenant' are a policy layer (Cedar or OPA) evaluated alongside, with forbid overriding. Audit every tuple write.

Follow-up: how do you handle a user removed from a group with 50,000 documents? — It's one tuple delete; the graph handles the fan-out at check time, which is exactly why ReBAC beats copying ACLs onto every document.
H
Your microservices each embed role checks like if user.role in ['admin', 'manager']. Plan a migration to a policy engine.

First inventory: extract every authorisation decision (grep for role checks, ownership comparisons, tenant filters) into a list of (service, endpoint, action, resource, rule). Define a resource and action vocabulary and a schema. Write policies in Cedar or Rego that reproduce today's behaviour exactly, and test them against recorded decisions. Introduce the engine in shadow mode: services call it alongside their existing code and log mismatches. Fix the policies or the bugs the mismatches reveal (you will find real IDOR bugs). Then switch each service to enforce the engine's decision, keeping default deny, and add a CI rule that new endpoints declare their action and resource. Finally, move volatile data (memberships, sharing) to a PIP the engine can query rather than tokens.

Follow-up: what's the biggest risk? — Data, not policy: policies are only as right as the attributes and relationships fed to them, so the migration must also decide where each fact lives and how fresh it is.
H
How would you implement time-bound, just-in-time access for engineers to production?

Default: no standing access. An engineer requests a role (for example db-read on payments) with a reason and duration; a policy decides whether it needs approval (on-call engineers may self-approve read access for 1 hour; write access needs a second person). On approval, the grant is written with an expiry — as a ReBAC tuple with a TTL, or an attribute 'elevated_until' evaluated by ABAC policy — and short-lived credentials are minted (au10). The policy checks now < expiry on every request, so access ends on time without cleanup jobs. Every grant, approval and action under it is logged and reviewed. Separation of duties: the approver can't be the requester.
refs: Zanzibar: Google's Consistent, Global Authorization System (USENIX ATC 2019)
Relation tuples, userset rewrites, zookies and the new-enemy problem, Leopard indexing, and production numbers.
Rego, policy testing, and deploying OPA as a library, sidecar or service.
Policy syntax, entities and schemas, and evaluation semantics (default deny, forbid overrides permit).
NIST SP 800-162: Guide to Attribute Based Access Control
ABAC concepts, PDP/PEP/PIP architecture and enterprise considerations.
Least privilege, deny by default, validating on every request, and testing authorisation logic.
An open-source Zanzibar-inspired authorisation system with a modelling language and playground.

t: Multi-tenancy and isolation: tenant IDs everywhere, row-level security, noisy neighbours, per-tenant keys and IDOR/BOLA
sum: Keeping customers' data and performance apart in shared systems: silo, bridge and pool isolation models, carrying tenant context from token to query, an IDOR bug and its fix, PostgreSQL row-level security with the connection-pool and owner-bypass traps, tenant-aware caches, queues, search and logs, noisy neighbours with quotas and shuffle sharding worked numerically, per-tenant encryption keys and crypto-shredding, and First American's 800-million-document exposure.
prereq: au1
Authorisation has function, object and property levels; object-level (IDOR/BOLA) is most often missing; the data layer can enforce a last line that fails closed.
au8
Decisions combine roles, attributes and relationships; list endpoints need authorisation as query filters; deny by default; test with other tenants' IDs.
db13
Connection pools reuse database sessions across requests; PgBouncer's transaction mode hands a connection to a different client after each transaction, so session state can leak.
sc7
Partitioning splits data by a key across shards; hot keys and skew cause uneven load.
sc12
Rate limiting, bulkheads and timeouts keep one source of load from exhausting shared capacity.
why:
For years, First American Financial — one of the largest title-insurance companies in the US — let customers view their documents through web links that contained a sequential document number. Change the number by one and you saw someone else's mortgage paperwork. No login was required. In May 2019 the journalist Brian Krebs reported that the system exposed hundreds of millions of documents going back to 2003: bank account numbers and statements, mortgage and tax records, Social Security numbers, wire transfer receipts, driver's licence images. The US Securities and Exchange Commission later put the count at more than 800 million document images, found that the company's own security staff had identified the vulnerability months before the journalist did but it never reached management, and fined the company $487,616.

That is the most direct form of a multi-tenancy failure: a shared system serving many customers, with nothing checking that the person asking for a record belongs to the customer who owns it. Most SaaS leaks are subtler — a cache keyed without the customer ID, a search index queried without a filter, a background job that forgot which customer it was working for — but the shape is identical. In a shared system, every layer must know whose data it's touching.

Multi-tenancy is how almost all software-as-a-service is built: one deployment, many customer organisations ("tenants"), sharing servers, databases and queues because that's what makes SaaS affordable. The senior question this topic answers is "how do you keep tenants apart?" — not just their data, but their performance and their failures. We'll compare the isolation models (database per tenant, schema per tenant, shared tables); follow the tenant ID from the token to the query; write an IDOR bug and fix it; enforce tenancy in the database with PostgreSQL row-level security, including the two traps that silently disable it; extend the boundary to caches, search, queues, files and logs; contain noisy neighbours with quotas and shuffle sharding, worked with real combinatorics; and use per-tenant encryption keys for blast radius and deletion. The Prep Console's per-user scoping — every row keyed by user_id — is the small version of the same idea.
primer:
The apartment building

Think of a block of flats. Every tenant shares the building's structure, plumbing, lifts and front door; that's what makes rent cheaper than a detached house. But each flat has its own lock, its own post box and its own meter, and the building manager's master key is kept in a safe and its use is logged. If the post boxes weren't labelled, or one flat's tenant could run the hot water for the whole building dry, or the lift went to any floor regardless of whose key you used, sharing would stop being acceptable.

A multi-tenant system is that building. Tenants share compute, databases and networks for cost; isolation is the set of locks, labels and meters that make sharing safe. There are three kinds of isolation to provide:

  • Data isolation: tenant A can never read or change tenant B's data, through any path.
  • Performance isolation: tenant A's load can't make the system unusable for tenant B (the noisy neighbour).
  • Failure isolation: a bug triggered by tenant A's data, or a bad deployment, affects as few other tenants as possible (blast radius).

The analogy has a limit worth stating: in a building, the locks are physical and the same for everyone. In software, every new feature is a new door, and someone has to remember to fit a lock to it. That's why the most robust designs make the boundary automatic — enforced by the framework, the data layer and the infrastructure — rather than relying on each developer remembering.

Who is "the tenant"?

A tenant is the unit you promise to keep apart. In business software it's the customer organisation — Acme's whole workspace, with all its users. In a consumer product it may simply be each user, which is how the Prep Console works: every learner's progress is private, so each user is effectively a tenant of one. Some products have two levels (a reseller with many end customers, or an organisation with many workspaces), and then isolation must hold at both. Naming the unit precisely matters, because it decides what goes in every key, filter and log line, and what you tell customers when something goes wrong.

A spectrum of sharing

How much to share is the first design decision. At one end, each tenant gets its own database (or its own deployment entirely): the silo model. In the middle, tenants share a database server but each has its own schema: the bridge model. At the other end, everyone shares the same tables, and every row carries a tenant_id: the pool model. (The names come from AWS's SaaS architecture guidance, and they're widely used.)

If you stop here: carry a verified tenant ID through every layer, make every data access filter by it — ideally enforced by the data layer so a forgotten filter fails closed — keep one tenant's load from hurting others, and test the boundary as seriously as you test features.
body:
1. Choosing an isolation model

Each model has a characteristic set of strengths and failure modes:

Silo (DB or stack per tenant)Bridge (schema per tenant)Pool (shared tables)
Data isolationinfrastructure-enforcedschema-level; same servercode- and RLS-enforced
Performance isolationstrongshared server resourcesneeds quotas and fairness
Cost per tenanthigh (idle capacity)mediumlow
Migrations× number of tenants× number of schemasonce
Per-tenant backup/restoretrivialpossiblehard (extract by tenant_id)
Data residency, CMKsnaturalpossibleneeds per-tenant keys
Typical failurerouting to the wrong databasesearch_path / schema mix-upsa missing WHERE tenant_id

Tenant count and size usually decide. Ten thousand small tenants in silos means ten thousand databases to patch, migrate and monitor; fifty enterprise customers with data-residency contracts in a shared table means difficult conversations with their auditors. Hence tiering: pool for the long tail, silo (or dedicated cells) for large or regulated tenants, with a tenant directory that routes each request to the right place.

2. Tenant context: from token to query

Every request must establish its tenant from something the client can't forge, then carry it to every layer:

  1. Authenticate the user (au3-au6). The token or session yields the user and either a tenant claim or a list of memberships.
  2. Select and verify the tenant. Users in several tenants pick one (a header, a subdomain such as acme.app.example, a path segment); the server checks the user is a member of that tenant on every request. A tenant ID from the request is a claim to be verified, never a fact.
  3. Bind the verified tenant into request context — a request-scoped variable the data layer reads — so handlers can't accidentally use a different one.
  4. Propagate it to everything the request causes: downstream service calls (in the internal token, au1), queued jobs (in the message, verified when consumed), log lines and traces (as a field), and the database session (section 4).

The Prep Console does the single-user version: the session yields uid, load_user() verifies it against the database on each request and stores the row in g.user, and every progress query takes g.user["id"] — never a user ID from the URL or body. Each user is, in effect, a tenant of one.

3. An IDOR bug and its fix

Here's the classic bug in a Flask-style API for a pooled invoices table:

@app.get("/api/invoices/<int:invoice_id>")
@login_required
def get_invoice(invoice_id):
    row = db.execute("SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = %s", (invoice_id,)).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        abort(404)
    return jsonify(dict(row))

Three faults. The lookup is by ID alone, so any logged-in user of any tenant can read any invoice: change 17 to 18 and Acme's user reads Initech's invoice — exactly First American's flaw, minus the missing login. The response returns every column (SELECT *), including internal fields such as cost price or notes the user's role mayn't see (property-level exposure, au1). And there's no audit of who read what.

The fix scopes by tenant in the query, returns 404 for invisible objects, selects only allowed fields, and checks the role:

@app.get("/api/invoices/<int:invoice_id>")
@login_required
def get_invoice(invoice_id):
    t = g.tenant                                   # verified from the session, never the request
    authorize(g.user, "invoice.read", tenant=t)    # function-level: role allows reading invoices
    row = db.execute(
        "SELECT id, number, amount, status, issued_at FROM invoices "
        "WHERE id = %s AND tenant_id = %s", (invoice_id, t.id)).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        abort(404)                                 # same answer for 'not yours' and 'missing'
    audit("invoice.read", resource=invoice_id, tenant=t.id)
    return jsonify(dict(row))

And the test that would have caught it, generated for every route that takes an ID:

def test_invoice_cross_tenant(client_acme, invoice_of_initech):
    r = client_acme.get(f"/api/invoices/{invoice_of_initech.id}")
    assert r.status_code == 404

Scoping by tenant in each query is necessary but fragile: one forgotten clause anywhere is a leak. The next section makes the database enforce it too.

4. Row-level security in PostgreSQL

Row-level security (RLS) lets the database add a filter to every query on a table according to a policy. For tenancy:

ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;          -- apply to the table owner too

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING      (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);

USING filters rows that queries can see, update or delete; WITH CHECK stops inserts or updates that would write a row for another tenant. If RLS is enabled and no policy applies, PostgreSQL shows no rows — default deny. The true argument to current_setting means "return NULL instead of an error if unset"; tenant_id = NULL is never true, so a request that forgot to set the tenant sees nothing rather than everything. Now the buggy handler above returns 404 for Initech's invoice even though its query forgot the tenant clause — the database added it.

The application sets the tenant at the start of each transaction:

BEGIN;
SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', '6f1c…acme-uuid', true);   -- true = local to this transaction
SELECT id, amount FROM invoices WHERE id = 18;                 -- returns nothing: 18 is Initech's
COMMIT;

Two traps silently switch RLS off, and both are common:

Trap 1: who bypasses RLS. Superusers and roles with the BYPASSRLS attribute always bypass it. The table owner bypasses it too unless the table has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. Many applications connect as the same role that ran the migrations and therefore owns the tables — so without FORCE, RLS does nothing for them. The robust setup is a separate application role that owns nothing, has no BYPASSRLS, and is granted only the privileges it needs, plus FORCE on every tenant table as a belt-and-braces measure.

Trap 2: connection pools. db13 explained that pools reuse database sessions. If the application runs SET app.tenant_id = 'acme' at session level and the pool — PgBouncer in transaction mode, or an application pool that doesn't reset state — hands that connection to the next request, which is for Initech and forgets to set its own tenant, the Initech request runs as Acme. Using SET LOCAL or set_config(…, true) inside a transaction scopes the value to that transaction, so it can't leak, and if a request forgets to set it, the NULL-means-nothing behaviour fails closed.

RLS has costs. Policies add predicates to every query, so tenant_id must lead the relevant indexes (it usually should anyway — composite primary keys like (tenant_id, id) keep each tenant's rows together). Functions used in policies should be simple and marked appropriately so the planner can use indexes. Some operations — cross-tenant maintenance jobs, analytics — need a separate, audited role that bypasses RLS deliberately. And RLS expresses tenant boundaries well but complex per-object authorisation poorly; it's a backstop for au8's checks, not a replacement.

5. Beyond the database

Data lives in many places besides the primary database, and each needs the tenant boundary:

  • Caches. Every key must include the tenant: t:acme:settings, not settings. A shared cache key is a cross-tenant leak that only appears under load. HTTP caches and CDNs need Vary or private caching for tenant-specific responses (net7).
  • Search indexes. Shared indexes store tenant_id on every document, and every query must filter on it inside the search engine (not by post-filtering results). Per-tenant indexes or aliases are an option for large tenants.
  • Queues and jobs. Messages carry the tenant; consumers set tenant context from the message before touching data, and validate it. A job runner that defaults to "no tenant" with an RLS-bypassing role is a classic leak.
  • Object storage. Prefix keys by tenant (s3://bucket/acme/…), grant service access by prefix, and make pre-signed download URLs short-lived. Never let a user-supplied path choose the prefix.
  • Analytics and warehouses. Copies of production data often lose RLS. Keep tenant IDs, restrict who can query across tenants, and audit it.
  • Logs, traces and error trackers. Payloads in logs mix tenants; restrict access, redact sensitive fields, and include tenant ID as a field so access can be scoped and incidents scoped.
  • AI features. Embedding stores and retrieval indexes are search indexes with the same rules; a shared vector index queried without a tenant filter will happily retrieve another customer's documents into a prompt. au12 covers permission-aware retrieval.

6. Noisy neighbours

Performance isolation fails in predictable places: one tenant's bulk import saturates database I/O; a tenant's report runs a full-table scan; a tenant's integration retries in a tight loop; a single huge tenant's queue backlog delays everyone else's jobs. The defences:

  • Per-tenant rate limits and quotas at the edge (sc12): requests per second, concurrent requests, payload sizes, storage, jobs in flight — sized by plan tier, with clear 429 responses.
  • Fair scheduling for shared work: per-tenant queues serviced round-robin, or weighted fair queuing, so a tenant who enqueues a million jobs waits behind themselves, not in front of everyone.
  • Database guards: statement timeouts, per-role connection limits, and moving heavy reporting to replicas or a warehouse.
  • Isolation for the largest tenants: their own pool, cell or silo.
  • Per-tenant metrics: you can't fix what you can't attribute — record tenant on resource usage so the noisy tenant is visible.

7. Shuffle sharding, worked

Sharding tenants across workers (sc7) limits how many tenants a worker failure affects, but everyone on a shard shares its fate: a tenant whose requests crash the process (a "poison pill") takes down every tenant on its shard. Shuffle sharding, described in the Amazon Builders' Library, gives each tenant a random combination of workers instead.

Take 8 workers. Plain sharding into 4 shards of 2 puts a quarter of tenants on each shard; a poison-pill tenant kills its shard and 25% of tenants go down. With shuffle sharding, each tenant gets a random pair of the 8 workers. There are C(8, 2) = 28 distinct pairs. When the poison tenant crashes its two workers:

  • Tenants with exactly the same pair lose everything: about 1 in 28 of them, 3.6%.
  • Tenants sharing one of the two workers lose half their capacity but stay up — if clients retry on their other worker.
  • Everyone else is unaffected.

Scale it: 100 workers with 5 per tenant gives C(100, 5) = 75,287,520 combinations. With 10,000 tenants, the expected number sharing the poison tenant's exact five workers is 10,000 ÷ 75,287,520 ≈ 0.00013 — effectively none. The insight is combinatorial: the number of possible shards grows enormously with small shard sizes, so correlated failures between tenants become rare without giving each tenant dedicated workers.

8. Per-tenant encryption keys

Encrypting data at rest with one key for everything protects against a stolen disk, not against a confused application. Per-tenant keys add three properties. Using envelope encryption (au11), each tenant has a data key that encrypts its data, and that data key is itself encrypted ("wrapped") by a key-encryption key in a key management service (KMS).

  • Blast radius: a leaked or misused data key exposes one tenant.
  • Customer control: enterprise customers can require a customer-managed key (CMK, sometimes "bring your own key") in their own KMS account. The service must call their KMS to unwrap the tenant's data key; the customer sees every use in their own logs and can revoke access, which stops the service reading their data.
  • Crypto-shredding: to delete a departed tenant's data from backups, replicas and logs you can't easily rewrite, destroy their key. Without it the ciphertext is noise. This is often the only practical way to meet deletion obligations across years of backups.

The costs are operational: a KMS call on the data path (cache unwrapped data keys in memory for minutes), key rotation per tenant, and an availability dependency — if a customer revokes their key or their KMS is down, their data is unavailable, by design.
deep:
Cells: isolating failures, not just data

Large SaaS providers increasingly run cell-based architectures: many complete, independent copies of the stack (each with its own databases, queues and services), each serving a subset of tenants, with a thin routing layer in front. A bad deployment, a poison-pill request or a database failure affects one cell's tenants. Cells also make tiering natural — an enterprise tenant can have a dedicated cell — and cap the size any one database must reach. The hard parts are the router (which must be extremely simple and highly available, since it's shared), moving tenants between cells, and cross-cell features such as global search or users who belong to tenants in different cells.

Tenant-aware identity

Isolation starts at login. In B2B products a user often belongs to several tenants, and the identity system must model memberships, roles per tenant and tenant-specific SSO (au6). Two bugs recur. The "tenant switch" bug: the UI switches to tenant B but an API keeps using the tenant from a token issued for tenant A, or vice versa, mixing data. And the "cross-tenant IdP" bug: tenant A's SAML connection asserts a user with an email in tenant B's domain, and the app logs them into tenant B. Both are fixed by treating tenant as part of the authenticated context, verified per request, and scoping IdP trust to each tenant's verified domains.

Side channels between tenants

Even with perfect access checks, shared infrastructure can leak information indirectly. Timing differences reveal whether an object exists. Shared caches can leak through timing ("is this URL cached?"). Unique constraints across tenants leak existence ("that email is already registered" on a global users table reveals another tenant's user). Aggregate features — "popular in your industry" — can expose another tenant's data if computed from too few tenants. Defences: per-tenant uniqueness where possible, uniform responses, minimum aggregation sizes (k-anonymity), and treating any cross-tenant computation as a data-sharing decision that needs review.

Cross-tenant vulnerabilities in cloud platforms

Cloud providers are the largest multi-tenant systems of all, and researchers have repeatedly found cross-tenant bugs in managed services — for example Wiz's 2021 "ChaosDB" report on Azure Cosmos DB, where a feature's misconfiguration exposed keys that could access other customers' databases. Two lessons carry over to any SaaS. Features added for convenience (notebooks, integrations, admin consoles) often run with broad internal privileges, so they're where tenant boundaries break. And the provider's response matters: rotating every potentially exposed credential and notifying affected tenants quickly is part of the design.

Migrating tenancy models

Products often start pooled and later need silos for large customers, or start with schemas and hit catalog limits. Moving a tenant is a data migration with a correctness bar of "zero cross-tenant rows": copy by tenant ID with change-data capture, verify with per-table counts and checksums, cut over routing in the tenant directory during a brief write freeze, and keep the old copy read-only until verified. Designing tables from day one with tenant_id in every primary key and every unique constraint makes this — and RLS, and sharding by tenant — far easier.

Canary tenants and continuous verification

Code review and tests check the paths you thought of. Continuous verification checks the ones you didn't. Seed a few canary tenants with distinctive marker strings in every field type — names, titles, file contents, embeddings — and continuously run, as other tenants, every read surface the product has: search, autocomplete, exports, notifications, AI answers, analytics dashboards. Any appearance of a marker outside its tenant pages someone. It's cheap, it catches regressions in layers that unit tests rarely cover (caches, indexes, async pipelines), and it turns "we believe tenants are isolated" into a measured claim you can show auditors.

Admin and internal tooling

Internal tools — support consoles, data-fix scripts, analytics notebooks — legitimately cross tenant boundaries, and they're where isolation is weakest because they're built quickly for trusted users. Treat them as products with their own authorisation: just-in-time, ticket-bound access per tenant, read-only by default, every action logged to the affected tenant's audit trail, and a deliberately separate database role that bypasses RLS only for those tools. A support console that can query any tenant with one search box is a breach waiting for one compromised employee account.

Compliance shapes architecture

Regulation turns isolation choices into requirements: data residency (EU tenants' data stays in EU regions), contractual deletion timelines (crypto-shredding), audit rights (per-tenant audit logs), and customer-managed keys for regulated industries. Mapping each requirement to a mechanism early — which tier gets silos, which regions, which key model — avoids retrofitting isolation into a pooled system under contract pressure.
prod:
How cross-tenant leaks actually surface

Usually from customers: "I can see another company's name in my dropdown." The causes are almost always in the secondary layers — a cache key, a search query, an autocomplete endpoint, an export job, a GraphQL resolver for a nested field. When it happens: disable the feature, identify every request that could have crossed (logs with tenant and resource IDs make this possible), notify affected tenants with facts, and add a regression test plus a structural fix (RLS, a mandatory tenant parameter in the data layer) rather than just patching the one query.

Signals to monitor

Any authorisation decision where resource tenant ≠ caller tenant (alert on one); per-tenant request rate, CPU, database time and queue depth (noisy-neighbour attribution); per-tenant error and latency SLOs, not just global ones (a global p99 hides one tenant's outage); 404 rates on ID-taking endpoints per caller (IDOR probing — First American's scraping would have shown as one client fetching many sequential IDs); canary-tenant markers appearing outside their tenant; and RLS configuration drift (a check that every tenant table has RLS enabled and forced).

Operational knobs

Quota sizes per plan tier; fair-scheduling weights; statement timeouts; the threshold at which a tenant graduates to a dedicated pool or cell; shuffle-shard size (larger shards give more capacity per tenant and more overlap); data-key cache lifetimes for per-tenant encryption (longer is cheaper, shorter honours CMK revocation sooner).

First American, as an engineering post-mortem

Krebs's May 2019 report described document links on First American's site containing a sequential number that could be incremented to retrieve other customers' documents without authentication, with records back to 2003. The SEC's June 2021 order says the EaglePro application exposed over 800 million images including Social Security numbers and financial information; that information-security staff had found the vulnerability months before the journalist's report but hadn't remediated it or escalated it to the executives responsible for disclosure; and the company agreed to a $487,616 penalty. The engineering lessons stack neatly: an object-level check on every document fetch would have prevented it; unguessable, expiring, recipient-bound links would have contained it; monitoring for sequential access would have detected scraping; and a vulnerability process that escalates critical findings with deadlines would have closed it months earlier.

Communicating with tenants

B2B customers increasingly ask, in security questionnaires, exactly how their data is isolated: which model, whether RLS or per-tenant keys are used, how support access works, and how a cross-tenant incident would be detected and disclosed. Being able to answer with mechanisms and evidence (test results, canary monitoring, audit logs) rather than assurances is part of the product.

Right-sizing again

The Prep Console is a pool of users in one SQLite file with owner scoping in every query and per-user deletion (DELETE FROM … WHERE user_id = ? across tables when an admin removes a user). With a handful of invited users there's no noisy-neighbour problem to speak of and no need for RLS, which SQLite doesn't have anyway. If it became a product for schools, each school would be a tenant, and everything in this topic would start to apply.
myths: Random UUIDs for object IDs prevent IDOR.

They make guessing harder, not access control correct. IDs leak through URLs, logs, emails, browser history, shared links and other APIs that list them. First American's document links used sequential numbers, which made scraping trivial, but the root fault was serving documents without checking who asked. Unguessable IDs are defence in depth; the check is the control.
Row-level security means the application can't leak tenant data.

PostgreSQL RLS is bypassed by superusers, roles with BYPASSRLS and, unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, the table's owner — which is often the role the application connects as. And the tenant variable it reads must be set correctly per request; with a transaction-mode connection pool, a session-level SET can leak one tenant's ID to another request. RLS is a strong last line only when those are handled.
A database per tenant is always the most secure option.

It gives strong data isolation and easy per-tenant restore, but shifts risk to operations: thousands of databases to migrate, patch, back up and connect to, and a routing layer that must never send a request to the wrong database — a mistake there leaks a whole tenant at once. The right model depends on tenant count, size, compliance needs and team capacity.
Tenant isolation is only about data.

Performance isolation matters just as much to customers: one tenant's bulk import or runaway query can slow everyone (noisy neighbour), and shared caches, queues and rate limits can leak data or starve others. Isolation covers data, compute, quotas, keys, logs and blast radius of failures.
If the token carries the tenant ID, we're safe.

Only if every layer uses it: the authorisation check compares it with the object's tenant, every query filters by it, caches key on it, background jobs carry it, and nothing accepts a tenant ID from request parameters instead. Most cross-tenant leaks happen in the layers that forgot to look.
lab:
Goal: reproduce an IDOR, fix it, simulate a pooled-connection tenant leak and the transaction-scoped fix, and check shuffle-sharding numbers — Python 3.12 standard library only (sqlite3, itertools, random, math). About 15 minutes.

  1. Data. In sqlite3 (in memory), create invoices(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, tenant TEXT, amount REAL) and insert rows for acme and initech.
  2. IDOR. Write get_invoice_v1(session, invoice_id) that ignores session["tenant"]. As Acme, fetch an Initech invoice. Then get_invoice_v2 with AND tenant = ? returning None → "404".
  3. Enforced filter. SQLite has no RLS, so emulate it: create views per tenant is awkward; instead write a TenantDB wrapper whose query(sql, params) refuses SQL that doesn't contain tenant = :tenant and always binds :tenant from its own context. Show the buggy query raising an error instead of leaking.
  4. Pool leak. Simulate a pool: a list of "connection" dicts holding a tenant setting. Request 1 sets it at "session level" and returns the connection; request 2 (Initech) forgets to set it and reads Acme's data through the wrapper. Then change to "transaction level": the wrapper clears the setting on release, and an unset tenant returns no rows.
  5. Shuffle sharding. With math.comb, print C(8,2) and C(100,5). Simulate 10,000 tenants each assigned random.sample(range(8), 2); pick a poison tenant and count tenants fully down, half down and unaffected. Repeat with 100 workers and 5 each.

What to look for: step 2's v1 returns another tenant's invoice although the user is logged in; v2 returns "404". Step 3 turns a forgotten filter into an exception — the "fail closed" property RLS gives in PostgreSQL. Step 4 reproduces the connection-pool leak and shows that clearing per-transaction state makes the forgetful request see nothing. Step 5 shows about 357 of 10,000 tenants (1/28) fully down with 8×2, and almost certainly none with 100×5.
recap: Multi-tenancy shares infrastructure between customers, so every request, query, cache entry, message, file and log line must carry and respect a tenant boundary.

Isolation models range from silo (separate stack or database per tenant) through bridge (schema per tenant) to pool (shared tables with tenant_id), trading isolation strength against cost and operability.
The tenant comes from the authenticated identity, never from a request parameter, and object lookups must be scoped by it so a foreign ID returns 404.

PostgreSQL row-level security enforces tenant filters in the database; it must be forced for the table owner, bypassed by no application role, and fed a tenant setting set with SET LOCAL inside each transaction.
Caches, search indexes, queues, object storage paths and analytics pipelines need the tenant in their keys and filters too — they're where forgotten boundaries leak.
Noisy neighbours are contained with per-tenant quotas and rate limits, fair scheduling, workload isolation for big tenants, and shuffle sharding to limit how many tenants share a failure.
Per-tenant encryption keys limit blast radius, enable customer-managed keys and allow crypto-shredding when a tenant leaves.
Test isolation directly: cross-tenant tests for every endpoint, a canary tenant whose data must never appear elsewhere, and alerts on any cross-tenant access.
glossary: Blast radius
How much is affected when something fails or is compromised.
BOLA / IDOR
Broken object-level authorisation / insecure direct object reference: returning or changing an object by ID without checking the caller may access it.
Bridge model
Tenants share a database server but each has its own schema or set of tables.
Canary tenant
A test tenant seeded with unique marker data whose appearance anywhere outside it signals a cross-tenant leak.
Cell-based architecture
Running many independent copies (cells) of the whole stack, each serving a subset of tenants, so a failure is confined to one cell.
Crypto-shredding
Making data unrecoverable by destroying the key that encrypts it, rather than finding and deleting every copy.
Customer-managed key (CMK / BYOK)
An encryption key the tenant controls in its own key-management account, which the service must use to access that tenant's data.
Envelope encryption
Encrypting data with a data key and encrypting that data key with a master key held in a KMS.
FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY
A PostgreSQL table option that makes RLS policies apply to the table's owner too.
KMS
Key management service: a hardened service that stores master keys and performs encryption operations with them (au11).
Noisy neighbour
A tenant whose resource use degrades performance for other tenants on shared infrastructure.
Pool model
All tenants share the same tables, distinguished by a tenant_id column.
Quota
A cap on how much of a resource a tenant may use: requests per second, storage, concurrent jobs.
Row-level security (RLS)
A database feature that filters rows per query according to policies, such as tenant_id equal to the current session's tenant.
SET LOCAL
A PostgreSQL command that sets a configuration value only until the end of the current transaction.
Shuffle sharding
Assigning each tenant a random small subset of workers so that few tenants share exactly the same subset, limiting how far one tenant's problem spreads.
Silo model
Each tenant gets dedicated resources: its own database, or its own whole deployment.
Tenant
A customer organisation whose users and data must be isolated from other customers in a shared system.
Tenant context
The verified tenant identifier carried with a request through every layer that handles it.
Tiering
Offering different isolation levels by customer tier, such as pooled for small customers and siloed for enterprise.
Weighted fair queuing
A scheduling method that serves each tenant's queue in proportion to a weight, so no tenant's backlog starves others.
drill:
Incident: "customer sees another company's projects in search"

Your pooled multi-tenant project tool (PostgreSQL with tenant_id columns, Elasticsearch for search, Redis cache, PgBouncer in transaction mode) gets a ticket: a user at Acme typed "roadmap" in search and saw a project titled "Initech 2027 roadmap". Database queries all include tenant filters according to code review. Investigate and fix.

Answer

Contain. Disable search (or force a tenant filter at the proxy in front of Elasticsearch) immediately. Preserve logs.

Hypotheses, most likely first. (1) The search query builder omits the tenant filter on some path — a new "global search" endpoint, autocomplete, or a query type where the filter is added as a scoring clause (should) rather than a filter (must). Check the actual query sent for that request ID. (2) The indexer wrote Initech's project into a document with Acme's tenant_id — for example a background job that lost tenant context and defaulted. Check the indexed document's tenant field. (3) A cache: search results cached under a key without the tenant (search:roadmap). Check Redis keys for that pattern. (4) Less likely for search, but check: a database session variable set at session level leaking through PgBouncer to the indexer.

Scope. From search logs, find all requests where returned documents' tenant differs from the caller's tenant during the exposure window; that list is who saw what. Notify affected tenants with specifics.

Fix structurally. Route all search through one client library that requires a tenant and adds it as a mandatory filter; use filtered aliases or per-tenant indexes for large tenants; prefix every cache key with tenant; carry tenant in job messages and set it from the message; use SET LOCAL for any session variables; add a CI test that runs every search endpoint as tenant A against data seeded only in tenant B and expects zero hits; add a production check that drops (and alerts on) any search hit whose tenant differs from the caller's.
qa: E
Compare silo, bridge and pool tenancy models.

Silo gives each tenant its own database or whole stack: strongest isolation, simple per-tenant backup, restore and data residency, but cost and operational effort scale with tenant count. Bridge shares a database server but gives each tenant its own schema: moderate isolation, migrations must run per schema, and thousands of schemas strain catalogs and tooling. Pool puts every tenant in shared tables with a tenant_id column: cheapest and easiest to operate at scale, but isolation depends entirely on every query filtering correctly, so it needs defence in depth such as row-level security. Many SaaS products tier: pool for small tenants, silo for large or regulated ones.
E
Show an IDOR bug and its fix.

Bug: GET /api/invoices/<id> loads Invoice by primary key after checking the user is logged in, and returns it — any user can read any tenant's invoice by changing the number. Fix: derive tenant from the authenticated identity and include it in the lookup — SELECT … FROM invoices WHERE id = ? AND tenant_id = ? — returning 404 when nothing matches, so 'exists elsewhere' and 'doesn't exist' look the same. Add property-level filtering for fields the role mayn't see, and a test that requests another tenant's invoice ID and expects 404.
Follow-up: why 404 rather than 403? — 403 confirms the object exists, which leaks information (for example that a competitor is a customer); 404 reveals nothing.
E
Where does the tenant ID for a request come from?

From the verified identity: a claim in the validated access token, the user's membership looked up from their session, or the hostname mapped to a tenant and then checked against the user's memberships. Never from a request parameter or body field the client controls, unless the server then checks the user belongs to that tenant — users who belong to several tenants select one, and the selection must be validated on every request.
M
How does PostgreSQL row-level security work for tenant isolation, and what are its traps?

Enable RLS on a table and create a policy, for example USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid) and WITH CHECK the same for writes; every query then has that predicate added, and with RLS enabled but no policy, no rows are visible. The application sets app.tenant_id at the start of each transaction. Traps: superusers and BYPASSRLS roles skip policies; the table owner skips them unless the table has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and apps often connect as the owner; a session-level SET with a transaction-pooling proxy can leave one tenant's ID on a connection the next request reuses, so use SET LOCAL or set_config(…, true) inside the transaction; and if the setting is missing, make sure the policy fails closed.
Follow-up: does RLS replace application checks? — No; it's a backstop that catches forgotten filters. The app still needs object, role and property checks that RLS can't express well.
M
List the places outside the main database where tenant data commonly leaks.

Caches keyed without the tenant (two tenants' /settings cached under one key); search indexes queried without a tenant filter; message queues and background jobs that lose the tenant context and run with a default; object storage paths without tenant prefixes or with pre-signed URLs that never expire; analytics and data warehouses where analysts join across tenants; logs and error trackers containing other tenants' payloads visible to support staff; exports and reports generated by jobs; and AI features — embeddings and retrieval indexes shared across tenants (au12).
M
What is a noisy neighbour and how do you contain one?

A tenant whose usage degrades others: a bulk import saturating the database, a report query scanning millions of rows, a burst of API calls exhausting a shared pool. Contain in layers: per-tenant rate limits and quotas at the edge (requests, concurrent jobs, storage); fair scheduling in shared queues (per-tenant queues or weighted fair queuing so one tenant's 1 million jobs don't sit ahead of everyone else's); per-tenant connection and statement limits in the database; separate pools or silos for the largest tenants; and shuffle sharding so a tenant's failure affects few others. Measure per-tenant resource use so you can see who is noisy.
M
Explain shuffle sharding with numbers.

Instead of assigning each tenant to one shard (so all tenants on that shard share its fate), give each tenant a random subset of workers. With 8 workers and 2 per tenant there are C(8,2) = 28 possible pairs, so a poison-pill tenant that crashes its two workers fully takes down only tenants with the same pair — about 1 in 28 of them — while others lose at most half their capacity and keep working via their other worker. With 100 workers and 5 per tenant there are about 75 million combinations; among 10,000 tenants the expected number sharing the exact same five is far below one. AWS describes using this for Route 53 and other services.

Follow-up: what does the client need for this to work? — It must retry on another worker in its shard when one fails; shuffle sharding limits correlated failure, and retries turn partial capacity into availability.
M
Why use per-tenant encryption keys?

Three reasons. Blast radius: a compromised data key exposes one tenant, not all. Customer control: enterprise customers can supply a customer-managed key in their own KMS, revoke it to cut off access, and see every use in their own audit logs. Deletion: when a tenant leaves, destroying its key renders all its data — including backups and replicas — unreadable (crypto-shredding), which is far easier than finding every copy. The cost is key management at scale: envelope encryption with a data key per tenant, wrapped by a KMS key, cached carefully, rotated, and a dependency on the KMS on the data path (au11).
H
Design tenant isolation for a B2B SaaS with 20,000 small tenants and 50 large enterprise tenants.

Tier it. Small tenants: pool model in sharded PostgreSQL, tenant_id on every row and in every primary key and index, RLS forced on all tenant tables as a backstop, tenant context from the token set with SET LOCAL per transaction, and a repository layer that refuses queries without a tenant. Large tenants: silo databases (or dedicated cells) for performance isolation, data residency and customer-managed keys, routed by a tenant directory. Everywhere: tenant-prefixed cache keys, search filtered by tenant in the engine, per-tenant queues or fair scheduling, per-tenant quotas, tenant-prefixed object storage with short-lived URLs, and audit logs with tenant on every event. Shuffle-shard the stateless tier. Test with canary tenants and cross-tenant tests in CI.

Follow-up: how do you move a tenant from pool to silo as it grows? — Copy its rows by tenant_id to the new database with change-data capture, switch routing in the tenant directory during a short write freeze, verify counts and checksums, then delete from the pool.
H
Walk through First American's 2019 exposure and what controls would have prevented it.

First American's EaglePro document-sharing application served documents from links containing a document number. Anyone with one link could change the number and retrieve other customers' documents — the SEC says over 800 million images dating back to 2003, including Social Security numbers and bank details — with no check that the viewer was entitled to that document. A journalist notified the company on 24 May 2019; the SEC later found its security staff had identified the vulnerability months earlier but it hadn't reached management, and the company paid a $487,616 penalty. Controls: object-level authorisation on every document fetch (link tokens bound to one document and recipient, expiring), unguessable IDs as defence in depth, rate limiting and anomaly detection on sequential access, and a vulnerability-management process that escalates critical findings.
Follow-up: how would you detect scraping like this? — Alert on a single client accessing many distinct document IDs, especially sequential ones, and on high 404/200 ratios across IDs.
H
A support engineer needs to view a customer's data to debug an issue. How do you allow it safely?

Make it explicit, scoped and audited. The engineer requests access to tenant T for a ticket; the customer (or a policy for severity-1 incidents) approves; the system grants a time-bound role, say read-only for 2 hours, recorded as a tuple or attribute with an expiry. All access during the window is tagged with both the engineer and the ticket, written to the tenant's own audit log, and visible to the customer. No standing cross-tenant access for anyone; the impersonation path goes through the same authorisation checks as normal requests, with the actor recorded separately from the subject. Break-glass access for emergencies triggers alerts and review.
H
How do you test that tenant isolation actually holds?

Several layers. Unit and integration tests per endpoint that create two tenants and attempt every operation with tenant A's credentials on tenant B's IDs, expecting 404, generated automatically from the route list so new endpoints are covered. Database tests that connect as the application role and confirm RLS hides other tenants' rows even for raw queries, and that FORCE is on. Canary tenants seeded with unique marker strings, with continuous scans of search results, caches, exports and logs for those markers appearing in other tenants' contexts. Production monitoring that alerts on any decision where the resource's tenant differs from the caller's. And periodic penetration tests focused on IDOR.
